research.abstract: Background: Individuals of African genetic ancestry are at high risk for heart failure (HF), which is often preceded by cardiac structural and functional abnormalities. Nevertheless, little is known about cardiac structure and function among Afro-Caribbeans residing in Tobago. This study aimed to investigate the epidemiology of cardiac structure and function among African Caribbeans in Tobago. Methods: A total of 924 participants (41-83 years) underwent clinical evaluation and transthoracic echocardiography. Images were analyzed for left ventricular (LV) mass index (MI), left atrial volume index, diastolic dysfunction (DD), LV ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e' ratio, E/A ratio, and other echocardiographic measures. Cardiac structure and function were evaluated by age, sex, and HF stage. Results: The mean age was 61.7 years, with 61.4% women, 47.8% obesity, and 20.2% diabetes. Average systolic blood pressure was approximately 140 mmHg, and 76.7% had hypertension. Abnormal LV geometry was present in 77.1% of participants, predominantly concentric remodeling (69.5%). The prevalence of DD was 13.4%, LVEF <50% was 1.5%, and abnormal GLS ([≤]-18%) was 5.2%. Women had significantly higher E/e' ratios and a higher prevalence of Stage A and Stage B HF, whereas men had a higher prevalence of symptomatic (Stage C) HF. Participants aged 65-83 years had significantly higher E/e' ratio, concentric remodeling, and LV hypertrophy than those aged 41-57 years. Conclusions: Women and older adults have higher LV structural abnormalities and DD than men and younger adults. These results will be helpful to inform public health priorities related to cardiovascular health in Tobago.

research.abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to increasing multidrug resistance (MDR). While acquired resistance mechanisms are well-documented, the genetic variability of intrinsic efflux pumps like EmrD remains less characterized. This study investigated the genomic diversity and structural conservation of the EmrD transporter in ten clinical MDR isolates from the Kurdistan Region, Iraq. Isolates were screened for the emrD and β-lactamase genes, followed by emrD sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and in silico protein modeling. Results confirmed the universal presence of emrD alongside multiple resistance genes. Phylogenetic analysis identified notable local genetic diversity, including a highly divergent lineage (DUH 11). Protein modeling mapped non-synonymous substitutions to transmembrane helices 6 and 12, regions critical for the "rocker-switch" conformational changes required for substrate translocation. These findings suggest that while EmrD is a stable component of the MDR machinery, localized genomic divergence may potentially influence efflux efficiency among clinical lineages, warranting future functional validation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. Brazil is among the 30 high-burden TB countries, however, genomic surveillance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains remains limited. We analyzed a convenience sample of 350 clinical isolates collected between 2016 and 2021 in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro to investigate genomic diversity, drug resistance and transmission dynamics. Among the isolates, 302 were phenotypically susceptible, while 48 showed resistance to at least one drug, including 35 multidrug-resistant (MDR) cases. Whole-genome sequencing predictions showed high concordance with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (rifampicin 99%, isoniazid 99%, ethambutol 98%, streptomycin 97%). The most common resistance mutations were katG Ser315Thr and rpoB Ser450Leu. All isolates belonged to Lineage 4, predominantly sub-lineages 4.1 (Haarlem) and 4.3 (Latin American-Mediterranean). Despite incomplete sampling, genomic analysis identified 28 transmission clusters involving 23.2% of isolates, including a large MDR-TB cluster in the Tijuca neighborhood. Multi-year clusters indicated continued detection of closely related isolates over time, suggesting the persistence of related genomic lineages. No association was observed between resistance-associated mutations and treatment outcomes, although these analyses were likely underpowered to detect such associations. These findings highlight the need to strengthen genomic surveillance, molecular diagnostics, contact tracing, and treatment follow-up to control TB in the region.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

research.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of resistance to five new and repurposed drugs (NRDs), identify risk factors for resistance, and characterize associated genetic mutations and transmission among people with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

research.abstract: Introduction Abutilon fruticosum Guill. & Perr. is a drought-tolerant Malvaceae subshrub native to Saudi Arabia. However, no mitochondrial genome has previously been reported for the genus Abutilon . This study reports the first complete mitochondrial genome of A. fruticosum and evaluates its comparative and phylogenetic relationships within Malvaceae. Methods The mitochondrial genome was assembled, annotated, and analyzed for genome composition, repetitive sequences, codon usage, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, synonymous and nonsynonymous substitution rates, collinearity, and phylogenetic relationships inferred from 32 shared mitochondrial protein-coding genes across ten taxa. Results The mitogenome was assembled as a circular molecule of 826,313 bp, with a GC content of 44.94%, and contained 37 protein-coding genes, 3 rRNA genes, and 21 tRNA genes. Comparative analyses of five Malvaceae mitogenomes revealed conserved codon-usage patterns, with weak-to-moderate bias influenced by nucleotide composition and functional constraints, but substantial variation in repeat abundance and distribution. DeepredMT predicted 397 RNA-editing sites in A. fruticosum , fewer than in Tilia amurensis , Gossypium trilobum , and Hibiscus cannabinus , but slightly more than in Adansonia perrieri . Simple sequence repeats and short dispersed repeats predominated, whereas G. trilobum had the greatest proportion of long repeats and H. cannabinus the highest repeat density. Nucleotide-diversity hotspots were detected in rpl16 , rps3 , cox2 , and rpl2 , while most protein-coding genes had dN/dS values below 1. The elevated dN/dS signal in rps4 suggested accelerated evolution or relaxed functional constraint, warranting further investigation. Maximum-likelihood analysis recovered A. fruticosum (tribe Malveae) as sister to the sampled Hibiscus – Gossypium clade with strong support. Discussion This study presents the first mitochondrial genome of Abutilon , expanding mitogenomic resources for Malvaceae. The A. fruticosum mitogenome shows conserved gene content and codon usage, alongside lineage-specific variation in repeat organization, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, and localized sequence divergence. The phylogenetic placement is consistent with the accepted classification of A. fruticosum in Malvoideae and illustrates the potential of mitogenomic data for systematic studies within Malvaceae, although broader taxon sampling is needed to test this placement. This mitogenome provides a resource for marker development, population-genetic studies, comparative mitogenomics, and phylogenetic research on Abutilon and related Malvaceae lineages.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) poses significant threats to animal health, public health, and wildlife conservation. Mycobacterium orygis, an emerging MTBC member, remains poorly characterized with respect to its epidemiology and transmission dynamics among Indian wildlife and livestock. METHODS: Fifty-five necropsy tissue samples from 21 captive wild animals were subjected to mycobacterial culture and a panel of molecular diagnostic assays, including multiplex PCR, Xpert-Ultra, and Truenat MTB/Rif. Confirmed MTBC isolates were characterized by drug susceptibility testing (GenoType MTBDRplus) and spoligotyping. Six isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and phylogenetic analyses were performed against publicly available reference genomes. RESULTS: Of 55 samples, 38 were MTBC-positive and 6 yielded nontuberculous mycobacteria. Drug susceptibility profiling revealed 28 pan-susceptible isolates, nine with isoniazid monoresistance, and one with rifampicin monoresistance. Spoligotyping classified 10 isolates as CAS1-Delhi, 27 as orphan lineages, and one remained unassigned. WGS of six isolates, representing diverse host species and tissue types, identified four as M. tuberculosis (CAS1-Delhi lineage). Notably, one orphan isolate from a blackbuck was reclassified as M. orygis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that this M. orygis strain was genetically distinct from other Indian wildlife strains and most closely related to a human-derived isolate from Karnataka, suggesting cross-host genomic relatedness. The remaining isolates clustered with Indian and global reference genomes; one was closely related to cattle-derived strains, whereas four were more closely related to human-derived strains. Low pairwise SNP distances (0-78 SNPs) with strong bootstrap support indicated close genomic relatedness across host species and geographic regions. CONCLUSION: This study shows the MTBC genomic diversity among various hosts. The phylogenetic relationships suggest that there is genetic relatedness among host populations such as M. orygis in a captive Indian blackbuck, which was in human contact for a long time. The study demonstrates the importance of integrated One Health genomic surveillance of mycobacterial infections at the human-animal interface and calls for more extensive, epidemiologically linked studies to look for cross-host transmission pathways.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding how species diversity originates, accumulates and is sustained across heterogeneous regions is a core goal of macroevolutionary and conservation biology. The genus Huperzia is an ancient and cosmopolitan lineage of lycophytes, with species widely distributed in both temperate alpine and subtropical low‐ to mid‐elevation areas, offering ideal material for investigating the diversification history of early vascular plant lineages. Here, we utilized 87 plastid genomes from 23 species to reconstruct a robust phylogenetic framework within Huperzia and found that the development of the petiole and midrib should be considered supplementary diagnostic characters in future taxonomic revisions. Our spatiotemporal and spatial phylogenetic analyses indicated that temperate and montane regions, especially northeastern China and parts of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, preserve phylogenetically distinctive paleo‐lineages, whereas subtropical evergreen broad‐leaved forests contain younger lineages associated with ecological expansion and trait differentiation. This niche transition was accompanied by repeated leaf‐trait differentiation and shifts in plastid‐gene selection in subtropical lineages, with three positively selected genes ( rps19 , chlB and atpH ) identified by branch‐site analyses. This evolutionary strategy provides a new perspective for understanding how early vascular plants maintained a dynamic equilibrium between refugial conservatism and adaptive innovation.

research.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate whether fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) combined with deep learning can detect metabolic signatures for classification of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). DesignCross-sectional analysis of participants included in the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with FLIO imaging. Subjects1,783 participants from the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with HbA1c measurements and FLIO imaging scans: 425 normoglycemic, 569 prediabetic, and 789 diabetic. MethodsGlycemic groups were defined from self-reported diagnosis, glucose-lowering medication, and HbA1c. Center-of-mass mean lifetime ({tau}CMM) maps, corrected for background and system timing offset, were generated from the raw time-resolved FLIO scans. Group differences in central-window {tau}CMM were tested by one-way ANOVA and by age-adjusted analysis of covariance. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ResNet-18, and XGBoost were trained on {tau}CMM maps for three-class (normal, prediabetic, diabetic) and two binary (normal vs. impaired; normal vs. diabetic) classification of T2DM and compared them with an age-only classifier and with models combining FLIO and age. Main Outcome MeasuresMacro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, F1 score, and positive predictive value (PPV). ResultsGroup-averaged {tau}CMM was longer in prediabetic and diabetic than in normoglycemic participants in both the SSC (p < 0.001) and the LSC (p < 0.001), but only the SSC difference remained significant after age adjustment (p = 0.017). For 3-class classification, the CNN using FLIO achieved the highest AUROC (0.60 {+/-} 0.04), compared with 0.51 {+/-} 0.03 for an age-only classifier. ResNet-18 and XGBoost showed similar performance. Binary classification of normal vs. diabetic participants yielded AUROC 0.67 {+/-} 0.04 (CNN), 0.64 {+/-} 0.04 (ResNet-18), and 0.62 {+/-} 0.04 (XGBoost). All three FLIO models exceeded the age-only classifier in all T2DM classification tasks, whereas adding age to the FLIO models did not improve model performance. ConclusionsFLIO-derived {tau}CMM maps capture retinal signals associated with diabetes status that exceed what age alone provides, but yield modest classification performance with current artificial intelligence models. These findings highlight both the potential and the challenges of using FLIO for early metabolic screening and monitoring, informing future development of clinically applicable imaging biomarkers.

research.abstract: Tetrigidae is an early-branching family of Caelifera whose species live on damp ground, feed largely on mosses, algae and detritus, and often show wing and pronotum polymorphism. Which chemosensory and detoxification genes underlie this lifestyle is unknown. We generated an Oxford Nanopore PCR-cDNA transcriptome from a pooled sample of adult Hyboella guangxiensis (4.25 million full-length reads) and used it, together with protein homology, to filter the 17,996 machine-learning gene models of its chromosome-level genome to 15,338 supported genes without loss of BUSCO completeness. For nine families (OBP, CSP, IR, SNMP, P450, CCE, GST, UGT, ABC), full-length transcripts corrected 28 of 447 loci, including split and fused models, and brought protein lengths into agreement with orthologs of the sister species Bolivaritettix circocephalus (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.00066). Only 251 loci were supported by complete-ORF transcripts, and 101 had no full-length reads at all. Reconciliation of family phylogenies across eleven orthopteran genomes assigned 119 well-supported duplications to the Tetrigidae stem branch, dominated by P450 (42), UGT (27) and ABC (22) genes, and identified 63 homologous groups restricted to Tetrigidae. Five lineage-specific groups detected as transcripts in adults were validated at the genome level in four non-tetrigid outgroups: a CYP301A-like array, a Tetrigidae-specific UGT clade, two Tetrigidae-specific chemosensory proteins, a CYP9E2-like array and an esterase FE4-like array. Branch-site tests found episodic selection on some members of the UGT and CYP301A-like groups and in 7 of 28 recent paralog pairs, but not in the CYP9E2-like, FE4-like or CSP groups. These genes are candidates for the cuticular, chemosensory and dietary adaptations of pygmy grasshoppers to be tested with tissue-resolved data, whereas no family member could be linked to wing polymorphism.

items.title: Multiple adaptive trajectories shape antimalarial resistance evolution in Ethiopian Plasmodium falciparum
items.summary: Plasmodium falciparum malaria continues to impose a substantial public health burden across sub-Saharan Africa, with Ethiopia experiencing a recent resurgence in malaria cases. We analysed whole genome data from 120 P. falciparum isolates collected in 2024 across five ecologically and epidemiologically diverse transmission settings in Ethiopia and placed these in the context of 1,220 publicly…

research.abstract: Abstract Plasmodium falciparum malaria continues to impose a substantial public health burden across sub-Saharan Africa, with Ethiopia experiencing a recent resurgence in malaria cases. We analysed whole genome data from 120 P. falciparum isolates collected in 2024 across five ecologically and epidemiologically diverse transmission settings in Ethiopia and placed these in the context of 1,220 publicly available genomes. Parasite populations were highly structured within Ethiopia, while Horn of Africa isolates formed a genetically distinct regional cluster relative to East and West African populations. We identified evidence of recent positive selection surrounding the artemisinin resistance associated Pf K13 R622I variant and detected co-occurrence with Pfcrt mutations together with recurrent selection signals at genes within the Pf K13-associated haemoglobin endocytosis pathway, including Pfmca2 , Pfkic7 , Pfkic8 and Pfkic9 . We further observed the emergence of the Pf PX1 D384A-PIN haplotype, with shared identity-by-descent linking Ethiopian and Ugandan carriers, supporting a recent introduction followed by local selection. Widespread Pfhrp2/3 deletions occurred on diverse genetic backgrounds. Together, these findings reveal a complex adaptive landscape shaped by antimalarial and diagnostic selection pressures and suggest that parasite evolution in the Horn of Africa proceeds through multiple adaptive trajectories, rather than through the spread of a single dominant lineage.

items.title: Natural selection on synonymous genetic variation in the major histocompatibility complex
items.summary: Protein coding DNA sequences harbor synonymous nucleotide variation that does not change amino acid sequences but influences phenotypes via multiple effects on the pathway from gene to protein. Synonymous variation has recently been shown to coevolve between viruses and their natural hosts, but its potential role in host immune defenses has not been explored. Here, I present evidence of natural…

research.abstract: Abstract Protein coding DNA sequences harbor synonymous nucleotide variation that does not change amino acid sequences but influences phenotypes via multiple effects on the pathway from gene to protein. Synonymous variation has recently been shown to coevolve between viruses and their natural hosts, but its potential role in host immune defenses has not been explored. Here, I present evidence of natural selection on synonymous variation in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), a highly polymorphic multigene locus that plays a crucial role in pathogen recognition by the adaptive immune system of vertebrate species. Using data from a wild population of Great Reed Warblers, I show that codon usage in exon 3 of MHC class I (MHC-I) genes is under strong purifying selection in 57 out of 87 codon sites. Scanning the Great Reed Warbler genome for tRNA genes revealed that, for most amino acids, bias towards preferred codons was associated with abundances of tRNA isotypes, indicating that the purifying selection is likely driven by selection for increased translational efficiency. However, spikes of synonymous variation appeared in 30 of the 87 sites in the MHC-I exon 3, and in those sites, codon usage bias and correlations with tRNA abundances were reduced. About half of these sites fall in CpG contexts, where cytosine deamination elevates the mutation rate; the other half do not, leaving the driver of much of the variation unexplained. The distribution of the spikes of synonymous variation showed no consistent association with structural domains of the MHC-I protein, nor with sites under positive selection for amino acid change, which are considered important for antigen binding properties. Intriguingly, the amount of synonymous variation in genotypes showed a positive correlation with Darwinian fitness, indicating that important evolutionary forces are at play that neutralize purifying selection in the 30 sites. From an ultimate perspective, the release of purifying selection among certain sites in MHC genes may indicate an arms race with pathogens, and I propose that the spikes of synonymous variation reveal a footprint of natural selection to escape inhibitory molecular interactions targeting MHC mRNA. I advance this RNA-level arms race as a novel axis of host–pathogen coevolution and a hypothesis to be tested directly. The fitness association is specific to synonymous variation, independent of amino-acid differences and the number of MHC alleles in genotypes, implicating selection on the synonymous variation itself rather than linked protein-level diversity. These results expose a previously unrecognized layer of selection in a key immune gene family and highlight the potential functional importance of synonymous variation in host–pathogen coevolution with direct implications for understanding susceptibility to infectious diseases. Significance Statement Roughly a quarter of DNA mutations carry no amino acid change, yet a growing body of evidence shows such synonymous variation can still shape how genes work. This study shows that genes of the major histocompatibility complex, central to how vertebrates detect infection, carry a hidden layer of natural selection acting on this synonymous variation, and that it is linked to individual fitness in a wild bird population. The findings suggest hosts and pathogens may be locked in an evolutionary arms race playing out beneath the level of protein sequence, with implications for how susceptibility to infectious disease is understood and studied.

items.title: Convergent and divergent patterns of holobiont evolution in co-distributed chemosynthetic symbioses
items.summary: Intraspecific variation in microbial symbioses is shaped by a variety of ecological and evolutionary processes. In geographically separated populations, divergence in genomic traits is expected due to dispersal barriers and habitat differentiation, whereas sympatric populations might exhibit functional convergence to the characteristics of a shared environment. While these two processes have been…

research.abstract: Abstract Intraspecific variation in microbial symbioses is shaped by a variety of ecological and evolutionary processes. In geographically separated populations, divergence in genomic traits is expected due to dispersal barriers and habitat differentiation, whereas sympatric populations might exhibit functional convergence to the characteristics of a shared environment. While these two processes have been well documented in many animal and plant species, they remain understudied in symbiotic systems. Here, we examined these processes in Atlantic cold seep mussel species that associate with environmentally acquired methane and/or sulfur-oxidizing bacteria. Using genomic methods, we reveal an eco-geographical barrier between the Western Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico that influences the distribution of symbiont species and the level of divergence between holobiont populations. While host populations were only slightly differentiated across this divide, symbiont populations were structured both between and within regions. The sulfur-oxidizing symbionts contained different regional types of dissimilatory nitrate reductase, possibly due to variation in oxygen availability. The methane-oxidizing symbionts showed evidence for convergent evolution, such as retention of a secondary, iron-dependent methane monooxygenase in Western Atlantic populations, driven by local copper limitation. These findings advance our understanding of divergent and convergent adaptive mechanisms underlying intraspecific host-symbiont variation in horizontally transmitted symbioses. Lay Summary Mussels of the subfamily Bathymodiolinae are foundation fauna at deep-sea cold seeps, where they rely on methane- and sulfur-utilizing bacteria for nutrition. Little is known about how these symbioses have evolved across large geographic ranges and varying environmental conditions, although it is thought that mussels typically partner with symbionts whose traits are suited for the specific characteristics at their local habitat. In this study, we collected samples of three co-occurring cold-seep mussel species across thousands of kilometers in the Western Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico and used genomic methods to compare both the mussel hosts and their symbiotic bacteria. Within each species, we found that, while mussel populations did not vary much genetically across the two regions, the genomic traits of the symbiotic bacteria differed between locations. For example, different symbiont species in the Western Atlantic independently shared a comparatively rare enzyme for methane utilization, likely because of the specific environmental conditions at seeps in this region. This observation suggests the occurrence of parallel adaptations across symbiont species, underscoring the importance of environmental pressures in driving the evolution of microbial symbioses.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Cardiovascular risk factors have changed in the United States, but trends in prevalence, management, and predicted risk through the post-pandemic period remain incompletely characterized. Methods We analyzed 11 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) periods (1999–2000 through 2021–2023) among 60,199 nonpregnant adults aged ≥20 years. Survey-weighted regression assessed age-standardized trends, subgroup differences, and measurement-change sensitivity. We assessed awareness, treatment, and control of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. PREVENT equations estimated 10- and 30-year risks among adults without self-reported cardiovascular disease (CVD). Results Obesity increased from 47.4% to 57.2% (odds ratio [OR] per decade, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.16–1.30), with class III obesity more than doubling (4.7% to 9.7%). Diabetes increased from 8.2% to 12.7% (OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.19–1.34), while current smoking declined from 24.4% to 14.9% (OR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.71–0.81). Hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, and prior CVD showed no significant linear trends, although mean systolic blood pressure (BP) (124.2 to 120.2 mm Hg) and total cholesterol (203.6 to 188.1 mg/dL) declined, alongside improvements in other lipids. Hypertension and dyslipidemia awareness and treatment increased, but BP control peaked at 32.5% in 2013–2014 before declining to 21.5%, while LDL cholesterol control rose from 17.0% to 34.2%. Diabetes awareness increased, but treatment trends were nonsignificant. Glycemic control peaked at 51.2% in 2003–2004 before declining to 41.9% (P for nonlinearity <0.001). Predicted 10-year total CVD risk declined from 5.66% to 5.28%; atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk declined by 0.16 percentage points per decade (95% CI, −0.22 to −0.09), while heart failure (HF) risk increased by 0.10 (95% CI, 0.03–0.17). Their 2021–2023 estimates were nearly identical (3.20% and 3.19%, respectively); 30-year risks showed similar divergence. Conclusions Improvements in smoking, blood pressure, and lipids coexisted with rising obesity and diabetes, declining blood pressure control after earlier gains, and divergent predicted ASCVD and HF risks.

items.title: The extracellular morphology and behaviour of the last common ancestor of animals and choanoflagellates
items.summary: Choanoflagellates, the closest known living relatives of animals, provide a powerful comparative system for investigating the evolution of extracellular morphology and cell behaviour on the animal stem lineage. Although all choanoflagellates share a conserved cellular architecture including a flagellum and collar of microvilli, they display a wide diversity of extracellular structures and…

research.abstract: Choanoflagellates, the closest known living relatives of animals, provide a powerful comparative system for investigating the evolution of extracellular morphology and cell behaviour on the animal stem lineage. Although all choanoflagellates share a conserved cellular architecture including a flagellum and collar of microvilli, they display a wide diversity of extracellular structures and behaviours throughout the life cycle. Their extracellular features, historically used for species identification, have long been suspected to reflect a mixture of evolutionary inheritance and ecological plasticity. Yet, the majority of choanoflagellate diversity remains undescribed, and the extent to which their extracellular traits map onto their phylogeny has remained unclear, impeding comparative reconstructions of the evolutionary history of extracellular structures with the earliest animals. Here, we integrate super-resolution fluorescence imaging, electron microscopy and transcriptomic analysis to characterize the extracellular structures and behaviours across both currently described lineages of choanoflagellates (Craspedida and Acanthoecida), by studying pairs of closely related species in conjunction with novel isolates representing previously unexplored clades. Our results reveal strong conservation of extracellular morphology between close relatives, whereas deeper evolutionary distances uncover unexpected innovations, such as sheath-like layers, bipartite thecae, crawling stages and atypical inverted division patterns. Furthermore, the inclusion of early-branching taxa sister to the loricates supports the hypothesis that the silicified extracellular lorica is a derived trait rather than an ancestral feature. Together, our findings suggest that the last choanoflagellate common ancestor possessed an organic non-silicified extracellular covering composed of one or more layers and that it was capable of both swimming and crawling behaviours, refining the cellular context from which animals evolved.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cultivated peanut ( Arachis hypogaea L.) is an allotetraploid crop (2n = 4x = 40) with an AABB genome that preserves extensive synteny between its two subgenomes. This characteristic, along with the availability of multiple genomic resources, provides a valuable framework for the comprehensive characterization of gene families and for inferring their evolutionary dynamics. Here we report a genome-wide analysis of the Dof transcription factor family in peanut (AhyDof), including phylogenetic inferences, gene structures, chromosomal locations, patterns of gene duplication, and expression analysis. Results ​A total of 66 non-redundant Dof genes (AhyDofs) were identified and unevenly distributed across the A and B subgenom​es. Comparative analyses revealed extensive conservation of gene structure, protein motifs, and chromosomal localization among homeologous genes inherited from the diploid progenitors, indicating that allopolyploidization contributed to family expansion while having a limited impact on gene diversification. Phylogenetic analyses placed AhyDofs within the four major angiosperm Dof lineages, supporting the evolutionary conservation of this family across flowering plants. Synteny analyses further identified chromosomal rearrangements and tandem duplication events contributing to the current composition of the AhyDof repertoire. Most notably, we discovered a novel group of six Dof genes associated with previously undescribed Pack-MULE transposons, designated AMuD, providing the first evidence of Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication in the genus Arachis . Structural and phylogenetic analyses suggested that these elements originated from non-autonomous MULEs and captured an ancestral Dof gene related to AhyDof-15.3. The dN/dS rate analysis suggested that transduplicated genes may have evolved under selective constraint, potentially indicating that functional constraints were maintained after mobilization. Comparative genomic analyses, PCR assays across diploid species, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing data suggested that AMuD elements originated within the B–F–K lineage of section Arachis and were maintained during peanut domestication and diversification. Promoter analyses revealed distinct cis-regulatory architectures among AMuD-derived genes, while transcriptomic data demonstrated their transcriptional activity, particularly in reproductive tissues. Conclusions The evolution of the peanut Dof repertoire in peanut was shaped by multiple mechanisms, including polyploidization, chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplication, and lineage-specific Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication. The discovery of AMuD elements reveals a previously undescribed mechanism contributing to the diversification of regulatory genes in Arachis and provides new insights into the evolutionary dynamics of plant transcription factor families.

items.title: BEAGLE 4.1: A high-performance library for computation on phylogenetic trees across diverse parallel architectures
items.summary: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations…

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND Active case finding (ACF) in India screens large populations to find few cases. AI-NETRA predicts neighbourhood-level tuberculosis (TB) risk from routine notification data and generates field microplans. OBJECTIVE To compare the yield and efficiency of AI-guided and standard ACF, and frontline acceptability. DESIGN Prospective quasi-experimental evaluation in four TB Units of Pune district, comparing two-week AI-guided sweeps (April to May 2026) with the routine campaign in the same units (December 2024 to January 2025). Primary endpoint: bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB per persons screened; secondary: all-forms yield, presumptive yield, referral precision, number needed to screen (NNS) and cost per case. Acceptability: 16 focus groups (n=100) and a survey of 101 ASHAs. RESULTS AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and confirmed 10 pulmonary cases, against 9 among 177,322 in the standard campaign (rate ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.09 to 8.29); NNS was 6,610 versus 19,702 and cost per case 66% lower. All-forms detection did not differ (15 versus 32; RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.39); the standard campaign had mobile X-ray. 96% of ASHAs reported finding the same presumptive cases while screening fewer people. CONCLUSION Geospatial targeting raised confirmed yield per person and lowered NNS; total detection did not differ. A concurrent, like-for-like trial is warranted.

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 18 loci (L = 26,700 aligned columns; Lagomorpha outgroups, Sciuromorpha, Castorimorpha, Dipodoidea, invasive Muridae, and New World Cricetidae: Arvicolinae, Neotominae, and Sigmodontinae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three North American PopSets (Peromyscus maniculatus, Sigmodon hispidus, and Urocitellus parryii; 3 × N = 36 = 108 conspecific isolates) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The continental radiation of rodents (Order Rodentia) across North America via Paleogene Beringian corridors, Miocene grassland expansions, and Great American Biotic Interchange exchanges—coupled with the Anthropocene introduction of Old World commensal murids—established both the foundational small-mammal trophic guilds of Nearctic ecosystems and the primary sylvatic reservoirs for North America's major rodent-borne zoonoses. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across an 18-locus, 64-species Glires supermatrix (L = 26,700 aligned columns with 7,979 parsimony-informative sites and 8,803 distinct site patterns) paired with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three conspecific North American population datasets (3 × N = 36 = 108 isolates) benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors the Glires root (Lagomorpha vs. Rodentia) at 65.2 Ma, Crown Rodentia at 56.8 Ma, the Sciuromorpha–Castorimorpha split at 36.4 Ma, Myodonta (Dipodoidea vs. Muroidea) at 46.5 Ma, the Muridae–Cricetidae divergence at 24.8 Ma, Crown Cricetidae at 18.6 Ma, and the New World Neotominae–Sigmodontinae split at 13.4 Ma. Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on the Sin Nombre hantavirus endothelial receptor ITGB3 beta-3 integrin (omega = 0.5319), intermediate selective constraint on the high-altitude and fossorial hypoxia axis EPAS1/HBB (omega = 0.0343) and rodenticide-detoxification locus VKORC1/CYP2C (omega = 0.2572), and diversifying positive selection on bacterial pattern-recognition receptors TLR2/TLR4 (omega = 0.2631) and the New World Arenavirus receptor TFRC transferrin receptor 1 apical domain (omega = 0.1453). Across the three single-species PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve post-glacial forest/oak-mast expansion and contemporary ENSO Sin Nombre hantavirus / Lyme disease amplification in the North American deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus, N = 36, Ne = 433,194 to 653,847; *BEAST = 667,970), northward agricultural grassland expansion and Black Creek Canal / Tamiami viral irruptions in the hispid cotton rat (Sigmodon hispidus, N = 36, Ne = 1,534,254 to 1,753,302; *BEAST = 1,808,005), and post-LGM Beringian steppe-tundra recolonization and high-latitude permafrost-thaw dynamics in the Arctic ground squirrel (Urocitellus parryii, N = 36, Ne = 707,606 to 1,687,680; *BEAST = 1,740,336), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 42.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.88 s vs. 595.24 s Hybrid and 1861.52 s full External UFBoot). This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A…

research.abstract: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 35 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates underwent WGS. Sequence data were quality-filtered and mapped to the H37Rv reference genome, characterising variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Lineage classification, drug resistance profiling, and identification of resistance mutations were performed using TB-Profiler software. SNP-based clustering was used to infer recent transmission events. All four major M. tuberculosis lineages (L1-L4) were detected; however, more than half of the isolates belonged to lineage L3 (CAS, n = 19; 54.3%). Almost all isolates were drug-resistant (34/35), including pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR, n = 15; 42.9%) and multidrug-resistant (MDR, n = 14; 40.0%) strains. The most frequent resistance-associated mutations included katG S315T (27/35) and inhA c.-777C > T (4/35) for isoniazid resistance, rpoB S450L (24/35) for rifampicin resistance, embB M306I/V (18/35) for ethambutol resistance, and gyrA D94G (8/35) and A90V (5/35) for fluoroquinolone resistance. Compensatory mutations were observed in rpoC and ahpC. Mutations associated with bedaquiline and clofazimine resistance (mmpR5 c.140dupA, c.138_139dupTG) were detected in single isolates. Interestingly, one isolate exhibited a deletion encompassing mmpR5, mmpL5, and mmpS5, potentially increasing bedaquiline susceptibility. Phylogenetic analysis using 6,635 genome-wide SNPs identified two transmission clusters with < 9 SNPs differences, suggesting ongoing local transmission. These results highlight the presence of drug-resistant M. tuberculosis strains in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, encompassing both globally recognised and novel resistance-associated mutations. Our findings underscore the critical need to integrate WGS into TB surveillance and control programmes in Pakistan to guide targeted interventions and curb the spread of resistant strains. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62482-7.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila , and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris , those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

research.abstract: Abstract Mafa is a critical transcription factor in pancreatic beta-cell biology, orchestrating insulin expression in response to glucose elevations. As a member of the large MAF protein family, MAFA’s stability and activity are intricately regulated by GSK3-mediated phosphorylation. To decipher the functional roles of these phosphorylations, we engineered knock-in mice ( Mafa 4A /+ ) in which MAFA is rendered non-phosphorylatable. In all Mafa 4A /+ animals, MAFA stability was markedly enhanced. Under high-fat diet (HFD) conditions, Mafa 4A /+ males rapidly developed glucose intolerance, which was attributed to impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed disrupted beta-cell identity, characterized by increased expression of MODY-associated genes and a delta-cell signature, suggesting beta-to-delta cell reprogramming, a hypothesis supported by lineage-tracing experiments. Conversely, Mafa 4A /+ females exhibited hypoglycemia and, with age, developed pronounced inflammatory cystic ducts including mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs). Strikingly, MAFA protein was also detected in MCN biopsies from female patients, linking our findings to human pathology. Our results unveil a sex-biased impact of GSK3-mediated MAFA phosphorylation. The male phenotype closely parallels the MODY-like diabetes observed in patients with MAFA S64F mutations, implicating defective phosphorylation in disease etiology. The emergence of MCNs in female mice suggests a novel role for MAFA stability or mutations in the pathogenesis of these enigmatic neoplasms, providing a fresh molecular hypothesis with clinical relevance.

items.title: Health Care Workload Impacts and Cost-Effectiveness of a Metabolomic Risk Score-based Health Check for Cardiometabolic Disease Prevention in Finland
items.summary: BackgroundPredictive metabolomics enables efficient early cardiometabolic risk detection, supporting proactive prevention over traditional reactive healthcare approaches. We evaluated the impact of a novel metabolomic risk score (MRS)-based health check on healthcare workload and long-term cost-effectiveness compared with current practices in Finlands working-age population. MethodsA de novo…

research.abstract: Abstract Background Predictive metabolomics enables efficient early cardiometabolic risk detection, supporting proactive prevention over traditional reactive healthcare approaches. We evaluated the impact of a novel metabolomic risk score (MRS)-based health check on healthcare workload and long-term cost-effectiveness compared with current practices in Finland’s working-age population. Methods A de novo individual-level microsimulation model was developed to estimate labour time and cost-effectiveness when identifying individuals at risk of cardiometabolic diseases (cardiovascular diseases; CVD or type 2 diabetes; T2D). The model used synthetic data on 256,372 Finnish individuals aged 50–54 years without prior CVD or T2D. From a societal perspective, three scenarios were assessed: 1) replacing the standard health checks with MRS-based health checks, 2) replacing standard health checks with MRS-based checks plus enhanced prevention, and 3) comparing enhanced standard checks with MRS-based checks plus enhanced prevention. Outcomes included time required to identify at-risk individuals, incremental cost-effectiveness ratio per QALY gained, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. Results MRS-based health checks substantially reduce workload, saving 193,140 hours for nurses and 2,843 hours for physicians over five years. The approach is likely cost-saving across all scenarios, with discounted long-term savings ranging from €27 million to €258 million. In scenarios 1–2, QALYs improve, with gains from 1,316 to 10,813. In scenario 3, no QALY gains are observed, and minor losses occur due to differences in baseline risk stratification. Conclusions MRS-based health checks in primary and occupational care reduce workload and are likely a cost-saving strategy with potential health outcome benefits in identifying individuals at risk of cardiometabolic diseases. Plain language summary Heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes are common and costly health problems. Finding people at risk early can help prevent these diseases. This study looked at a new blood-test-based health check and compared it with current health checks in Finland. Researchers used a computer model based on over 250,000 people aged 50–54. They tested different ways of using the new test and compared time, costs, and health outcomes. The results suggested that the new test can save time for nurses and physicians and reduce healthcare costs. In most cases, it also improved health outcomes. This means that using this type of test could help healthcare services work more efficiently and support earlier prevention, which may benefit both individuals and society in the future. Funding This work was supported by Nightingale Health Plc.

items.title: Two Axes of Sleep, One Heart: Dissociating Objective Sleep-Disordered Breathing From Subjective Sleep Duration in Cardiac Risk
items.summary: Background: Cardiovascular epidemiology has long treated "sleep" as a single exposure, although it denotes both an objective physiological state and a subjective behaviour. We tested whether these domains carry separable information about cardiac risk. Methods and Results: We derived an objective axis from 8,444 polysomnograms (Sleep Heart Health Study) and a subjective axis of self-reported…

research.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular epidemiology has long treated "sleep" as a single exposure, although it denotes both an objective physiological state and a subjective behaviour. We tested whether these domains carry separable information about cardiac risk. Methods and Results: We derived an objective axis from 8,444 polysomnograms (Sleep Heart Health Study) and a subjective axis of self-reported duration from 407,303 adults in the 2020 and 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Multivariable regression (n=213,489), quadratic dose-response modelling, sleep-stratified comorbidity networks, and era-stratified tests were combined. Objective sleep-disordered breathing was continuous and right-skewed (median apnea-hypopnea index, 31.8 events/h; median sleep efficiency, 69%) in a risk-enriched cohort. Both short (<7 h) and long (>9 h) sleep were associated with disease after full adjustment: adjusted odds ratios for heart attack were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.19-1.30) and 1.30 (1.19-1.42), and for stroke 1.12 (1.06-1.17) and 1.42 (1.29-1.57). A positive quadratic term confirmed a U shape for all 4 outcomes formally tested (P≤6.3×10 2 ), with fitted nadirs of 7.26 to 7.85 hours. Suboptimal sleep also raised comorbidity-network density from 0.089 to 0.112 (short sleep; +26%) and 0.108 (long sleep; +22%), with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs and concordant effects across demographic strata. A survey-weighted replication in official CDC microdata (n=344,010; median design effect, 4.43) preserved the principal cardiac, U-shaped, and network findings; an exploratory COVID-19 interaction (P=0.020) did not survive design-based correction. Conclusions: Objective breathing pathology and subjective duration are separately prognostic, and suboptimal sleep amplifies the cardiometabolic comorbidity network. Duration alone cannot exclude asymptomatic sleep-disordered breathing; cardiovascular prevention should assess both axes.

items.title: An atlas of human histological diversity
items.summary: Descriptions of tissues by histopathologists rest on verbal statements limited by quantitative inaccuracies and personal cognitive biases. Here we propose an unsupervised computational framework that transposes to histology the concepts and methods of RNA-seq gene expression analysis, setting histology on an unbiased quantitative ground. Leveraging this framework and the GTEx dataset, we built an…

research.abstract: Descriptions of tissues by histopathologists rest on verbal statements limited by quantitative inaccuracies and personal cognitive biases. Here we propose an unsupervised computational framework that transposes to histology the concepts and methods of RNA-seq gene expression analysis, setting histology on an unbiased quantitative ground. Leveraging this framework and the GTEx dataset, we built an atlas surveying the histological diversity of 40 organs from 946 non-diseased individuals and documenting 11,125,747 associations between 2,560 morphemes - the histological analogs of genes in our framework - and 9 layers of patho-clinical and multi-omic molecular data, providing a rich context to interpret histology. In contrast with the ideally healthy normal specimens depicted in histology textbooks, the atlas reveals the influence of age, sex, genetics and sub-clinical pathologies on tissue structures. For example, we report that female eccrine sweat glands are surrounded by more adipocytes than their male counterparts, and that distinct calcification-associated aorta morphemes are driven by either smoking or genetic polymorphisms. Cross-organ analyses also delineate the systemic histological impact of diabetes and other conditions and establish the power of blood gene expression to predict disease-related morphemes. The atlas is released as an interactive web resource aimed at researchers.

items.title: Evaluation of urine lipoarabinomannan and host response signatures for culture-negative tuberculosis using composite criteria and Bayesian Latent Class Analysis
items.summary: Abstract Background: Culture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine…

research.abstract: Abstract Background: Culture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). Methods: Urine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated for each assay based on three reference criteria: composite microbiological, composite clinical, and a latent class model. Results: Positive classification proportions were 0.29 (32/112) and 0.46 (51/112) for the composite criteria and 0.20 (22/112) for the latent class model, with the Bayesian model estimating a prevalence of 0.31 (95%CrI 0.11-0.64). Sensitivity and specificity for uLAM ranged from 0.06-0.13 and 0.92-0.96, respectively. Sensitivity and specificity for HRS ranged from 0.47-0.78 and 0.56-0.69, respectively. uLAM results were significantly associated with microbiological positivity (OR=5.38, 95%CI=1.63-13.02). Conclusion: Three distinct reference frameworks identified different individuals as having culture-negative TB while producing index assay sensitivity and specificity estimates with overlapping confidence and credible intervals, leading to similar conclusions regarding biomarker utility. This supports the use of complementary reference approaches to assess robustness to disease classification uncertainty in heterogeneous conditions such as culture-negative TB.

Fine mapping by linkage and large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has narrowed this region to a 30-kb interval encompassing the ARMS2 and HTRA1 genes. research.abstract: Abstract Purpose The human 10q26 locus is a major genetic risk factor for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Fine mapping by linkage and large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has narrowed this region to a 30-kb interval encompassing the ARMS2 and HTRA1 genes. However, the causative gene(s), risk variants, and underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain unresolved. Methods Long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) candidates within the ARMS2–HTRA1 region were identified using human postmortem retinal RNA-seq data and public databases (NCBI, Ensembl). Candidate transcripts were validated by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing. Published single-cell RNA-seq datasets were analysed to define cell type–specific expression, and RNA levels were compared between AMD and non-AMD donor retinas. Additionally, expression changes were assessed in human iPSC-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells exposed to cigarette smoke extract (CSE) and paraquat (PQT). Results We identified and characterized the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) HTRA1-AS1 and its transcript variants within the ARMS2 locus. HTRA1-AS1 overlaps ARMS2 and is transcribed in the antisense orientation. It is predominantly expressed in rod photoreceptors, Müller glia, and choroid/RPE tissues. Retinal HTRA1-AS1 expression was significantly reduced in AMD donors compared with controls (43 AMD vs. 44 controls, P = 0.007), whereas HTRA1 mRNA expression showed no significant difference (P = 0.121). In induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells, cigarette smoke extract (CSE)-induced oxidative stress markedly increased HTRA1-AS1 and ARMS2 expression by up to 8-fold and 75-fold, respectively, whereas paraquat treatment produced no significant changes. Conclusion These findings identify HTRA1-AS1 as an AMD-associated lncRNA within the ARMS2 locus that exhibits cell-type-specific expression, disease-associated downregulation, and responsiveness to cigarette smoke-induced oxidative stress. These results suggest that HTRA1-AS1 may contribute to AMD pathogenesis through noncoding regulatory mechanisms, warranting further functional investigation.

items.title: RAMP-Seq: a single-tube nanopore workflow for co-amplifying full-length 16S rRNA and antimicrobial resistance genes for integrated taxonomic and resistance profiling
items.summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance needs workflows that both identify bacteria and detect resistance genes from a single sample, but current targeted nanopore assays typically split these steps into separate reactions or library preparations. We introduce RAMP-Seq (Rapid AMR Profiling by Sequencing), a workflow that simultaneously amplifies the full-length 16S rRNA gene (~1,500 bp)…

research.abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance needs workflows that both identify bacteria and detect resistance genes from a single sample, but current targeted nanopore assays typically split these steps into separate reactions or library preparations. We introduce RAMP-Seq (Rapid AMR Profiling by Sequencing), a workflow that simultaneously amplifies the full-length 16S rRNA gene (∼1,500 bp) together with eight resistance determinants (∼600–700 bp) in a single multiplex PCR and then sequences the resulting mixed-length amplicon pool as a single nanopore library. The eight-primer pair set targets dominant alleles of β-lactamase, carbapenemase, quinolone-resistance and silver-resistance families. Read-length distributions confirmed that both size classes were co-amplified evenly using a single, non-equimolar primer pool. From extracted DNA to the first taxonomically classified reads took 8.2 ± 0.6 h. Full-length 16S sequencing of an eight-member mock community identified all anticipated taxa, and the observed abundances closely followed the expected log-scaled composition (Pearson’s r = 0.879). The full nineplex amplicon assay was subsequently tested on three distinct matrices: pooled clinical isolates, spiked human blood, and environmental water samples. Using an equal-mass pool of genomic DNA from eleven multidrug-resistant clinical and repository isolates, the full assay produced genus-level and resistance-gene profiles that were consistent across biological replicates ( r = 0.998 and r = 0.824), and it specifically identified all seven panel targets present, confirmed by Illumina whole-genome sequencing. After carbonate-based host DNA depletion, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from spiked human blood at every titration down to 10² CFU/mL, as were all five panel targets carried by that strain. Across five water-sampling sites from a sewage treatment plant (STP) to a connected lake system, microbial communities and resistance-gene profiles were site-specific: influent and effluent communities overlapped little, while the lake inlet and outlet were similar. Target resistance genes were most numerous and abundant in STP influent, fewer in effluent, and rare or absent in lake and well samples. Because bacterial identification relies on amplification of the conserved, near-universal 16S rRNA gene, rather than on species-specific primer sets, RAMP-Seq can detect and taxonomically classify bacteria in a design-agnostic manner. The same single-tube chemistry therefore serves sample types as different as clinical specimens and environmental water and is extendable to longer ribosomal targets and further resistance-gene families. Impact statement Antimicrobial resistance surveillance must simultaneously identify bacteria and their resistance genes, but most sequencing workflows require separate reactions. This limits throughput and increases costs, constraints especially relevant for low- and middle-income settings. RAMP-Seq combines both tasks in one multiplex PCR, amplifying full-length 16S rRNA for identification plus eight resistance-gene targets, then sequencing them together as a single nanopore library on a portable MinION. From extracted DNA to first classified reads takes ∼8 hours, and one barcode per sample means a 12-barcode kit supports 12 samples. We successfully applied RAMP-Seq on multidrug-resistant clinical isolates, bacteria spiked into human blood, and wastewater and freshwater samples. Because it relies on a universal bacterial marker, it is not limited to predefined species, enabling use when pathogens are unknown, and lab capacity is limited. Data Summary All sequencing datasets produced in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession PRJNA1483527. Oxford Nanopore reads include the multidrug-resistant clinical isolate pool (two biological replicates; SRR39373345–SRR39373346); environmental water collected from five locations across a sewage treatment plant and the connected lake system (14 runs including technical replicates; SRR40992843–SRR40992856); and Klebsiella pneumoniae spiked into human blood at 10⁶–10¹ CFU/mL (two biological replicates per dilution; accessions SAMN64748836–SAMN64748837). Supplementary Tables S1–S10 contain culture-based identification and antimicrobial susceptibility results for the clinical isolates ( S1 ), environmental site descriptions and coordinates ( S2 ), sequences of the panel primers and of primers excluded during development ( S3–S4 ), primer concentrations ( S5 ), in silico coverage of the primer panel ( S6 ), summaries of sequencing runs and replicates ( S7) , Illumina whole-genome sequencing results ( S8 ), read-length binning statistics ( S9 ), and genus-level profiles of environmental samples ( S10 ). All data, materials, and protocols required to reproduce the results are available in the article, the supplementary materials, and the repositories listed above.

Here, we report high-quality chromosome-level genome assemblies of four representative Coptis species (C. chinensis, C. deltoidea, C. omeiensis, and C…

research.abstract: Coptis species belong to the Ranunculaceae family and have important pharmacological activity because their rhizomes are rich in isoquinoline alkaloids. However, the genome evolution and species relationships of Coptis remain poorly understood. Here, we report high-quality chromosome-level genome assemblies of four representative Coptis species (C. chinensis, C. deltoidea, C. omeiensis, and C. teeta). We found that the evolution of this group was strongly affected by geological events, especially the uplift of the Tibetan Plateau and the collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates. The triploid C. deltoidea exhibited striking B subgenome expression dominance, while C. omeiensis showed extensive tandem duplication of NLR disease-resistance genes. Rhizome branching and swelling were closely associated with the activation of brassinosteroid biosynthesis and signaling pathways. Key gene families involved in alkaloid biosynthesis were significantly expanded in Coptis and were mainly highly expressed in the rhizome. Multiple transcription factor families, including MYB, bHLH, and ERF, were identified as candidate regulatory factors associated with alkaloid biosynthesis. We further constructed the first public multi-omics database for Coptis. This study provides key genomic resources for understanding Coptis evolution, adaptation, and molecular breeding.

items.title: R-pyocin-mediated selection restores aminoglycoside sensitivity in a pan-drug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
items.summary: The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged…

research.abstract: Abstract The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged not as conventional biocides but as precise selective forces to drive an evolutionary trap. We subjected the laboratory strains PAO1 and PAK and the clinical pan-drug-resistant (PDR) wound isolate MRSN 6220 to R-pyocin selective pressure. Under sustained R-pyocin pressure, every pyomelanogenic variant we recovered evaded R-pyocin killing through large-scale chromosomal deletions spanning 250-388 kbp. These deletions encompass a conserved region harboring the galU gene (essential for LPS synthesis), the hmgA gene (yielding a pyomelanogenic ‘brown’ phenotype), and the mexXYZ multidrug efflux operon. While the loss of galU confers broad cross-resistance to R-pyocins by likely truncating the LPS receptor, the concurrent excision of mexXY induces profound collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides. These deletions also eliminate critical virulence factors and biofilm clusters, including the hcnABC , exoY , phzABCDEFG , and cup operons. In a Galleria mellonella model, the resulting brown mutants were non-lethal, and in infected murine wound tissue treated ex vivo with gentamicin they exhibited a significant 3-log reduction in bacterial load, whereas the pan-drug-resistant ancestor did not. This work establishes a framework for utilizing R-pyocins as evolutionary steering agents that couple the acquisition of R-pyocin resistance to the reversion of multidrug resistance into an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state. Importance Pan-drug-resistant (PDR) pathogens demand novel strategies that both kill and restore antibiotic efficacy. Here, we describe an evolutionary trap for Pseudomonas aeruginosa , where selection for R-pyocin resistance drives large-scale (∼300 kb) chromosomal remodeling. Although these deletions confer R-pyocin immunity via loss of the galU gene, they simultaneously collapse the pathogen’s virulence and defense. Crucially, the excision of the mexXY efflux operon resensitizes a PDR clinical isolate to conventional aminoglycosides, while the collateral loss of critical virulence and biofilm clusters abrogates pathogenesis. By coupling resistance acquisition to substantial fitness costs, our work establishes a framework for using R-pyocins to force predictable evolutionary trade-offs, driving the reversion of multidrug resistance to an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state.

research.abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a major challenge in tuberculosis control, and the occurrence of resistance in patients without any prior treatment history raises concern about the transmission of resistant strains within the community.We report the case of a 63-year-old woman presenting with cough for more than two months, marked weight loss, and intermittent fever, without any previous tuberculosis treatment or known contact with a tuberculosis patient.She had a history of diabetes mellitus.Physical examination revealed bronchial breath sounds with rhonchi, and chest radiography revealed infiltration at the right upper lung apex.Rapid molecular testing detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis with resistance to rifampicin, and second-line drug susceptibility testing further revealed additional resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolone, and ethionamide, leading to a diagnosis of primary pre-extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis.Random blood glucose was elevated and was managed with insulin, while mild hypochromic anaemia was managed with iron supplementation.The patient received bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, and remained clinically stable without significant adverse effects after one week of therapy.This case highlights the importance of vigilance for primary drug-resistant tuberculosis and the role of rapid molecular testing in early diagnosis and appropriate treatment selection.

research.journal: bioRxiv: the preprint server for biology
research.abstract: Abstract Codon-based maximum likelihood models are the workhorse of molecular selection analysis, yet standard workflows assume that the input sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree are known without error. In practice, heuristic aligners ignore the genetic code and phylogeny, which packs non-homologous codons into shared columns across insertion-deletion loops and inflates gene-wide false-positive rates above 80%. This sequential division of labor is statistically suboptimal and computationally wasteful. Here, we present WALRUS ( W heatstone A lignment and L ikelihood R ate U nification for S election), a unified engine in H y P hy 3 ( https://github.com/veg/hyphy-3 ) that maps unaligned coding sequences to a coordinate-consistent selection atlas in one run. From a single Inside–Outside likelihood table, the pipeline repairs reading frames, co-estimates a codon alignment and Ohmic reticulate network, models directional base-composition drift, and evaluates eight selection tests (BUSTED-E, aBSREL, RELAX, FEL, dFEL, MEME, Contrast-FEL, and PRIME). Across 10,020 simulated alignments, WALRUS recovers 94.6% of true columns on the 800 INDELible replicates and cuts indel-driven false positives from 44.7%– 58.1% to 4.4% under BUSTED (21.1%– 21.4% to 1.4% under BUSTED-E). Under Zipfian indel saturation, false positives drop four-fold (33.3%– 83.3% to 17.0%– 20.5%), while 11, 190 avian orthogroup runs execute 6.6–35.8-fold faster and cut housekeeping false positives 13-fold (28-fold on ultraconserved genes) proteome-wide.

Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from…

research.abstract: Abstract Background Whole-genome sequencing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) commonly relies on culture-derived isolates, potentially altering the bacterial populations represented. Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from participants initiating treatment for rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Worcester, South Africa. We assessed sequencing performance, technical reproducibility, sputum-sampling variability, lineage and variant concordance, and resistance-associated variation, and explored associations with baseline clinical characteristics and treatment response. Results Of 218 clinical dsWGS reactions, 139 passed sequencing quality criteria, yielding 113 eligible baseline sputum–culture pairs. Mixed-lineage infection was detected in 72/113 (63.7%) sputum specimens versus 7/113 (6.2%) matched cultures; 66/113 (58.4%) pairs showed reduced lineage diversity following culture. Permutation analysis indicated preferential retention of Lineage 2 and depletion of Lineage 3 after culture. Technical replicates preserved dominant phylotype assignments (median SNP Jaccard similarity 0.863), while independently collected sputum specimens showed greater variability. Among 38 concordant single-lineage pairs, 35,540/38,311 (92.8%) pair-specific variant observations were shared after filtering and raw-read recovery, while 2,497 (6.5%) were sputum-unique and 274 (0.7%) culture-unique. Discordance was concentrated among variable variants; 88.0% of shared variants variable in at least one specimen had higher allele frequencies in culture. No sputum-unique WHO Grade 1 or 2 resistance-associated mutations were identified in the strain-controlled subset, whereas eight mixed-lineage sputum samples versus three matched cultures harboured such mutations. Higher baseline low-frequency variant burden showed non-significant trends towards delayed culture conversion (log-rank p=0.144) and unfavourable treatment outcomes (log-rank p=0.400). Conclusions Direct-sputum WGS revealed M. tuberculosis lineage and low-frequency variant diversity that was not fully represented by matched culture-derived genomes, despite high overall genomic concordance. These findings highlight the complementary value of direct-sputum sequencing for characterising within-host diversity, while suggesting that the representation of bacterial populations following culture may vary across epidemiological settings. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of minority-variant detection and establish the clinical relevance of diversity measured directly from sputum.
