research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 16 loci (L = 23,924 aligned columns; African Catarrhini and Neotropical Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three independent PopSets (Alouatta spp., Sapajus/Cebus, and Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The colonization of South America by African anthropoid primates during the Middle to Late Eocene and their subsequent diversification across Neotropical forest strata into five ecologically specialized families (Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) represent one of mammalogy's classic trans-oceanic adaptive radiations. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across a 16-locus, 64-species primate supermatrix (L = 23,924 aligned columns with 10,254 parsimony-informative sites and 11,093 distinct site patterns) coupled with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three localized Neotropical population datasets benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors Crown Primates at 74.0 Ma, the trans-Atlantic Simiiformes split between African Catarrhini (crown 28.5 Ma) and Neotropical Platyrrhini at 43.2 Ma (stem rafting window 43.2–24.2 Ma across the Eocene Atlantic), and Crown Platyrrhini at 24.2 Ma, followed by crown radiations of Pitheciidae (19.8 Ma), Atelidae (16.8 Ma), Cebidae (19.5 Ma), Callitrichidae (14.8 Ma), and Aotidae (11.4 Ma). Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on Pro8-oxytocin OXT/OXTR neuroendocrine signaling (omega = 0.4905), intermediate selective constraint on TAS2R bitter-taste receptors (omega = 0.7442) and ENAM/GHR dental and phyletic-dwarfism loci (omega = 0.8436), and diversifying and balancing selection on duplicated RNASE1/CHIA folivory-insectivory digestive enzymes (omega = 1.2118) and X-linked OPN1LW spectral-tuning opsin exons (omega = 2.4891). Across the three localized PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve late Quaternary trans-Andean expansion and contemporary yellow fever epizootic pressure in howler monkeys (Alouatta, Ne = 628,056 to 977,186; *BEAST = 1,007,674), Pleistocene Cerrado/Caatinga dry-corridor colonization and stone-tool nut-cracking persistence in capuchins (Sapajus/Cebus, Ne = 1,042,598 to 1,376,278; *BEAST = 1,411,397), and Atlantic Forest fragmentation followed by metapopulation translocation recovery in callitrichid marmosets and tamarins (Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus, Ne = 469,859 to 912,085; *BEAST = 940,542), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 29.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.54 s vs. 404.82 s Hybrid and 3127.88 s full External UFBoot). research.abstract: Abstract Background The HSP70 family maintains cellular proteostasis and mediates vertebrate responses to environmental stress. The Chinese alligator ( Alligator sinensis ), an ectothermic crocodilian, undergoes winter dormancy characterized by cessation of feeding, reduced activity, and metabolic depression. However, the evolutionary patterns of the HSP70 family across vertebrates and their potential relevance to winter dormancy in crocodilians remain poorly understood. We characterized the HSP70 family across 24 vertebrate species, focusing on the molecular evolution of HSPA12A along crocodilian lineages and its seasonal expression in the hypothalamus of the Chinese alligator. Results Using HMMER- and BLAST-based searches, we identified 355 HSP70 family members, with 11–28 members per species. Phylogenetic, synteny, and subcellular localization analyses indicated that the family is broadly conserved but exhibits subfamily- and lineage-associated divergence. Under two foreground schemes in which the terminal branches of two winter-dormant crocodilians or all four crocodilian species were jointly designated as foreground, HSPA12A showed an elevated relative evolutionary rate and significant evidence of positive selection. HyPhy aBSREL supported episodic diversifying selection on the A. sinensis HSPA12A terminal branch. Public RNA-seq data showed that HSPA12A expression was highest in the hypothalamus among sampled female tissues and was higher in winter than in summer (600.0 and 329.2 TPM, respectively). Western blotting and immunofluorescence analyses showed descriptive differences between the examined specimens, with higher HSPA12A protein abundance and a higher density of cells double-positive for anti-HSPA12A antibody immunoreactivity and NeuN in winter. Because each RNA-seq, western blotting, and immunofluorescence comparison included only one biological specimen per season, these observations were treated as descriptive, and no inferential statistical comparisons were performed. Conclusions The vertebrate HSP70 family is broadly conserved but shows differentiation among subfamilies and lineages. The evolutionary analyses indicate a broader crocodilian-lineage-associated pattern of HSPA12A evolution that cannot be attributed specifically to winter dormancy. Separately, the descriptive transcriptomic and preliminary protein-level observations provide a basis for considering HSPA12A as a candidate for further investigation in relation to winter physiology in the Chinese alligator. These findings do not establish winter dormancy as the selective driver of HSPA12A evolution, and its biological function and causal role remain to be determined.

research.abstract: Camelids have evolved remarkable physiological adaptations enabling survival in extreme desert environments, yet the genomic basis of these traits remains incompletely understood. We conducted a comparative genomic analysis across eleven mammalian species, including three Old World camels, four New World camels, two additional artiodactyls (pig, cattle), and two outgroups (human, mouse), to identify lineage-specific molecular signatures of adaptation. Using OrthoFinder, we constructed orthologous gene families and identified 11,861 single-copy orthologs across all species. We detected significant copy-number changes in cytochrome P450 gene families, with expansion of CYP2J and contraction of CYP4F in the camelid ancestor, suggesting a shift toward anti-inflammatory eicosanoid signaling. Branch-site analyses identified 47 high-confidence positively selected genes in Old World camels, including HACD3, a fatty acid elongation enzyme harboring an ultraconserved substitution (D270N). Structural modeling and conservation analysis suggest that this substitution may hypothetically alter protein conformation, but this prediction awaits experimental validation. Tissue-specific RNA-seq analysis confirmed that HACD3 is expressed in camel kidney and liver, tissues central to lipid metabolism and water conservation. Systematic screening for inactivating mutations identified ten high-confidence pseudogenized genes, including CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, enriched in lipid metabolism and epidermal pathways. The adaptive significance of these losses is currently hypothetical and inferred from homologous gene studies in mice and humans; because some of the cited genes are paralogs rather than orthologs, and because mouse and human phenotypes may not transfer to camels, these inferences are hypothesis-generating only and do not establish camel gene function. Experimental validation confirmed pseudogenization of TAS2R16, and cell-based calcium-signalling assays showed that the camel receptor fails to respond to salicin. This establishes loss of receptor function but not its adaptive significance; both dietary-breadth and neutral (relaxed-selection or drift) explanations remain compatible with the data. For CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, functional consequences in camels remain unverified and require camel-specific experimental validation. Collectively, these results provide a comprehensive framework of gene family evolution, positive selection, and gene loss underlying desert adaptation in camelids, while highlighting that expression patterns are correlative only and do not demonstrate that the identified variants alter protein function or physiology.

research.abstract: Adaptive evolution frequently proceeds through the co-option of pre-existing biological functions, yet the molecular mechanisms by which such co-option generates new adaptive traits over contemporary evolutionary timescales remain poorly understood. Herbicide-resistant weeds provide a powerful model for addressing this question because enhanced herbicide metabolism has repeatedly evolved within only a few decades. Here, we show that resistance to cyhalofop-butyl in Echinochloa crus-galli evolved through the co-option of EcNIT4A2 , which encodes a nitrilase that normally functions in ethylene-associated cyanide detoxification. Genetic mapping, transcriptomics and transgenic analyses identified EcNIT4A2 as the major determinant of resistance. A D317G substitution enhanced its herbicide-detoxifying activity. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that this substitution facilitates substrate access to the catalytic pocket. A promoter structural variant markedly increased EcNIT4A2 expression. Our findings reveal how coding and regulatory changes can jointly drive the co-option and optimization of a conserved metabolic function during rapid adaptation under intense anthropogenic selection.

research.abstract: Abstract CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas greedy distance-based alternatives scale efficiently but their accuracy requires distances that faithfully represent the true phylogeny. Here, we introduce HERACLES, which optimizes cell coordinates in hyperbolic space under a quartet-based composite likelihood of CRISPR editing. By recovering local branching structures directly from embedded distances, HERACLES guides continuous optimization with an explicit evolutionary model without repeatedly constructing and evaluating complete phylogenies. Across simulated benchmarks, HERACLES improves reconstruction accuracy over existing methods and scales to lineages containing 150,000 cells in about four hours on a single GPU. On experimental KP-tracer and PEtracer datasets, HERACLES reconstructs phylogenies consistent with independent anatomical annotations and temporal lineage markers. Its flexible likelihood framework also accommodates different recording mechanisms, and incorporating sequential editing improves reconstruction of simulated DNA Typewriter lineages. Together, these results establish continuous optimization of local evolutionary relationships as a scalable and flexible approach to probabilistic lineage reconstruction. Code availability HERACLES is available at https://github.com/morrislab/HERACLES .

research.abstract: Abstract Background Dosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations. Methodology A pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to 10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80–125% of adult area under the concentration–time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility. Results Proposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10–14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25–39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6–24.9 kg. Conclusions A harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed. Author Summary Leprosy continues to affect children in many low-resource settings, yet guidance on how to dose treatment in younger children remains limited. Current recommendations often require clinicians to calculate mg/kg doses, which can be difficult in practice and may not match the oral formulations that are available. In this study, we used computer-based simulations to develop a simplified dosing approach for the three drugs used to treat leprosy. We showed that grouping children into weight bands, rather than calculating individual doses, can achieve drug exposures similar to those seen in adults, where treatment is known to be effective. Importantly, we found that these doses can be delivered using existing pre-packed treatment kits by removing selected dose units, making this approach practical in routine care. This work provides a more straightforward and reliable way to treat children with leprosy, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving access to treatment. However, challenges remain, including the lack of child-friendly formulations and limited data on how these drugs behave in children. Further studies are needed to improve treatment for this vulnerable population.

research.abstract: IntroductionAntimicrobial resistance (AMR) to first line antibiotics for pneumonia is a major global health problem, and AMR-attributable deaths are prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa. Improved data on how AMR develops and influences health outcomes in resource limited settings is crucial. The nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their resistome, the genetic determinants of AMR. No study has explored whether human resistome composition in children with pneumonia is associated with health outcomes. This study will examine whether antibiotic treatment and hospital admission for pneumonia generate a persistent hospital-acquired nasopharyngeal resistome in children, and whether this is associated with re-hospitalisation. MethodsThis is an observational case-control study, that will recruit 350 children aged 12-36 months from four groups in Blantyre, Malawi: healthy children in the community (healthy community), children with pneumonia treated in the community (community pneumonia), children hospitalised with pneumonia (hospital pneumonia) and children re-hospitalised with pneumonia (re-hospitalised pneumonia). Nasopharyngeal swabs will be taken at recruitment and 3-month follow-up study visits for metagenomic sequencing to characterise the nasopharyngeal microbiome and resistome; urine samples will be taken at recruitment for an antibiotic activity bioassay. Socio-demographic data, co-morbidities, pneumonia severity, antibiotic exposure and health outcomes will be recorded. AnalysisCross-sectional comparisons between groups at recruitment will examine whether nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) composition differs by pneumonia severity, antibiotic and healthcare exposure. Longitudinal comparisons within groups will assess the dynamics of NPR composition over time. The study is powered to detect a medium effect size (Cohens D = 0.505) change in the relative abundance of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) between all four groups. Primary outcomes are the difference in beta diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index), and relative abundance of ARG classes in the NPR. The primary objectives are to estimate the difference in diversity and relative abundance of the NPR between hospitalised pneumonia participants when compared to 1) healthy community and 2) community pneumonia participants, and to investigate whether participants re-hospitalised with pneumonia within a 3-month period have a persistent hospital-acquired NPR pattern. Ethics and disseminationThe study has been approved by the Kamuzu University of Heath Sciences Research Ethics Committee (KUREC, formerly Malawi College of Medicine Research Ethics Committee; Ref: P.10/24-1200) and Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine Research Ethics Committee (LSTM REC; Ref: 24-076). Trial registration numberISRCTN64027792 STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDYO_ST_ABSStrengthsC_ST_ABSO_LIStudy design that uses metagenomic deep sequencing to enable direct, concurrent comparison of nasopharyngeal microbiome (NPM) and resistome (NPR) composition between community and hospitalised paediatric populations with pneumonia in a resource-limited setting. C_LIO_LIData on reported and urinary bioassay-detected antibiotic use prior to, and throughout the study, enabling detailed examination of antibiotic selective pressure on the NPR. C_LIO_LIInvestigation of the association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes from pneumonia. C_LI LimitationsO_LILimitations to this study include few sampling time points (two for community pneumonia and three for hospitalised pneumonia), which may not fully capture the impact of antibiotic exposure; the potential for residual confounding following adjustment for known potential confounders (e.g. age, sex, co-morbidities, household exposure to smoke and breastfeeding) in the association between resistome composition and adverse clinical outcomes, for which the authors have detailed statistical analysis measures; and ability to only determine association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes, rather than causal inference, due to the case-control study design. C_LI SUMMARYO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSThe nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their genetic determinants of antibiotic resistance in children. Studies of nasopharyngeal microbiome composition have shown association with paediatric pneumonia severity and mortality. What this study addsThis study will describe nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) evolution under selective pressure of antibiotics and hospitalisation for paediatric pneumonia, and explore whether NPR composition is associated with health outcomes in a resource-limited setting. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThis exploratory study could inform larger scale observational studies to examine the association between antibiotic resistance and health outcomes, by defining high-risk nasopharyngeal resistome composition, helping to determine the required sample size and contributing open-source bioinformatic pipelines. The study could also inform research for public health interventions, including antibiotic stewardship.

We show that somersaulting pigeon brains exhibit mitochondrial redox dysfunction and identify an 11-bp frameshifting deletion in GLRX2, a mitochondrial redox enzyme, that abolishes protein function and is highly-enriched in two…

research.abstract: Darwin described the somersaulting behavior of pigeons as "one of the most remarkable inherited habits ever recorded", yet its molecular basis remained unknown. We show that somersaulting pigeon brains exhibit mitochondrial redox dysfunction and identify an 11-bp frameshifting deletion in GLRX2 , a mitochondrial redox enzyme, that abolishes protein function and is highly-enriched in two independently selected breeds. GLRX2 deficiency in mice and zebrafish recapitulates mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress and impaired motor coordination seen in pigeons. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identifies cerebellar Golgi and Purkinje cells as selectively vulnerable, with disrupted inhibitory signaling and synaptic remodeling. These findings demonstrate how relaxation of purifying selection during domestication can expose a deleterious mitochondrial variant to artificial selection, allowing gene loss to serve as a substrate for behavioral evolution.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Synonymous codon usage bias (CUB) provides a complementary perspective on molecular variation, but its relationship with morphological diversity in rapidly radiating plant lineages remains poorly understood. We investigated this relationship in Thelypteridaceae by integrating chloroplast phylogenomics, codon usage analyses, and published descriptions of lamina base architecture. A phylogeny based on 31 shared protein‐coding genes provided the evolutionary framework for 37 plastome accessions, including two outgroups. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) revealed three major codon usage groupings (Types A–C) that partly differed from the chloroplast phylogeny, with Types A and C corresponding descriptively to contrasting lamina base forms. A focused comparison of 27 accessions and eight genes retained this Type A–Type C separation. Although ENC, PR2, and neutrality plots showed broadly similar overall patterns between the types, gene‐wise analyses highlighted ndhJ, psaA, and psbD, and protein‐guided codon alignments reproduced their type‐specific synonymous third‐position counts. These complementary observations support a relationship between chloroplast codon usage variation and frond architecture in the sampled taxa. They identify candidate photosynthesis‐related loci and provide a basis for testing the evolutionary and functional processes underlying this relationship.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Bacteria of the order Mycobacteriales, including the genera Mycobacterium and Corynebacterium , possess a unique outer membrane, termed the mycomembrane, which is structurally and chemically distinct from the lipopolysaccharide-containing outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. A defining feature of the mycomembrane is its enrichment in mycolic acids, long-chain α-branched, β-hydroxylated fatty acids that occur as trehalose monomycolate (TMM), trehalose dimycolate (TDM), or are esterified to arabinogalactan, an unusual polymer that is itself covalently linked to peptidoglycan (PG). Mycoloyltransferases are Mycobacteriales - specific enzymes described to catalyze the transfer of mycolic acids from trehalose monomycolate (TMM) to various cell envelope acceptors, including trehalose and arabinogalactan. In several species, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis , these proteins are essential for viability; however, their occurrence as multiple paralogs with partially redundant functions has hindered the precise assignment of their cellular roles. Previously, we showed that Corynebacterium glutamicum remains viable in the absence of mycolic acids, and thus without a mycomembrane, following deletion of pks , the gene required for mycolic acid biosynthesis. Building on this finding, we systematically deleted all genes encoding mycoloyltransferases in C. glutamicum to further disclose their collective function in the cell. The resulting Δ myts mutant lacked arabinogalactan-bound mycolates and TDM, and continued to synthesize TMM. While this major outer membrane glycolipid is highly abundant, the Δ myts strain failed to assemble a mycomembrane and displayed pronounced cell aggregation. Deletion of mycoloyltransferases also caused very severe defects in cell division and morphogenesis that are not observed in a Δ pks strain unable to synthesize mycolic acids. Together, these results demonstrate that mycoloyltransferases are essential for mycomembrane assembly but dispensable for TMM biosynthesis, and reveal an important role for these enzymes in cell division that is independent of their canonical mycolic acid transfer activity. SIGNIFICANCE How the mycomembrane is assembled and anchored to the cell wall remains a central question in Mycobacteriales, where this outer membrane is necessary for envelope integrity and intrinsic antibiotic resistance. By genetically separating mycolic acid synthesis from their incorporation into the outer membrane, we identify arabinogalactan-linked mycolates as the critical determinant for initiating membrane assembly. Importantly, we also uncover a role for mycoloyltransferases beyond their canonical function in lipid metabolism, revealing a functional link with cell division. These findings point to a critical role of Mycoloyltransferases in the coordination between outer membrane biogenesis and bacterial cytokinesis.

research.journal: Otago University Research Archive (University of Otago)
research.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects the lungs and causes the disease tuberculosis, which the World Health Organization estimates causes 1 million deaths across the globe annually. Emergence of drug resistance has lessened the effectiveness and requires a longer duration of treatment. Bedaquiline was approved by the FDA in 2012 to treat multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis cases when no other treatment was viable. TBAJ-587, a derivative of Bedaquiline, has been found to be more effective at treating multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis, and has fewer adverse effects. The aim of this project was to test if strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis that have a mutation in Rv0678 causing overexpression of the MmpS5L5 efflux pump will evolve high-level resistance to TBAJ-587 at a higher frequency than wild-type strains. This was done by growing a wild-type M. tuberculosis strain and a ∆Rv0678 mutant on plates of 7H11 agar containing increasing concentrations of TBAJ-587, then selecting isolates and confirming resistance using an anti-microbial susceptibility assay to determine the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration of the isolated strains. 72 strains from the wild-type background were assayed, and 114 from the ∆Rv0678 background were assayed. The resistant ∆Rv0678 strains tended to have higher minimum inhibitory concentrations that the resistant WT strains. Mutations in the WT strains were found throughout Rv0678, and D28, E6, A62 and I66 mutations in atpE, as well as L168 in atpB. Similar atpE mutations were found in ∆Rv0678, with the addition of mutations in A63 of atpE.

items.title: Network-level selection constrains the adaptive evolution of gene expression noise in regulatory genes in changing environments
items.summary: Gene expression levels vary from cell to cell, even between clonal cells in identical environmental conditions. This variance is termed "expression noise" and is partially genetically encoded and subject to selection. While gene expression noise is detrimental in constant environments where the expression level is under stabilizing selection, it can be beneficial in changing environments, when…

research.abstract: Abstract Gene expression levels vary from cell to cell, even between clonal cells in identical environmental conditions. This variance is termed “expression noise” and is partially genetically encoded and subject to selection. While gene expression noise is detrimental in constant environments where the expression level is under stabilizing selection, it can be beneficial in changing environments, when the phenotype is far from the optimum. However, expression noise propagates along the gene regulatory network, making the evolution of connected genes interdependent. Here, we explore how the position of the gene in the gene network constrains the evolution of its expression noise and expression mean under selection using in silico evolution experiments. We simulate the evolution of populations of model gene regulatory networks under directional and fluctuating selection on the gene expression level while allowing the basal expression level and expression noise level to mutate. We find that expression noise is only transiently favoured under directional selection, indicating a co-evolutionary dynamic between expression mean and noise during adaptation. On the other hand, high levels of noise are persistently maintained under fluctuating selection. Furthermore, target genes, regulated by other genes, were more likely to respond to selection and increase their gene-specific expression noise than regulator genes. These findings show that not just the mean, but also the variance of gene expression level, respond to selection in changing environments, and do so in a network-dependent manner. They further point to gene expression noise as a mechanism for populations to escape extinction by creating phenotypic heterogeneity when faced with environmental changes.

research.abstract: Abstract Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag comprises two complementary methods: mFrag-Weight, which uses DNA methylation information to weight fragmentomic features, and mFrag-Net, which integrates fragmentomic features and external DNA methylation data through neural networks. We average the output probabilities of the two methods to obtain a final prediction score. The mFrag model was trained using 287 individuals at risk for lung cancer. In an independent case-control testing set comprising 385 non-cancer controls and 46 cancers (28 stage I, 12 stage II, and 6 stage III or IV), mFrag outperforms a DELFI-style fragmentomic approach, improving PR-AUC from 0.455 to 0.720 and sensitivity at 99% specificity from 0.043 to 0.478, with ROC-AUC from 0.871 to 0.908. For stage I lung cancer, mFrag raises PR-AUC from 0.314 to 0.558 and ROC-AUC from 0.855 to 0.894. Applied to end 4-mer motif features, mFrag likewise improved over an unweighted baseline, with gains contributed by both mFrag-Weight and mFrag-Net. In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.

items.title: Extracting and Updating Compact Colored k-mer Indexes
items.summary: Colored k-mer indexes record, for every k-mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new…

research.abstract: Abstract Colored k -mer indexes record, for every k -mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new genomes keep arriving. Rebuilding the index after every such change requires the original sequences and repeats the costly construction. We show that colored indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) can instead be updated efficiently in batches, without the original sequences, and with a result equivalent to the index built from scratch. Given an SBWT and any subset of its k -mers, we first extract the SBWT of this subset directly from the input, in one linear pass and without building a new index. Removing genomes, intersection and difference all reduce to this operation. We then carry the colors through every operation, by finding from the inputs alone where the color sets of the result change, so that removing or extracting genomes, as well as the union, intersection and difference of two colored indexes, each directly yield a complete colored index. In our experiments, editing paid off for large results: removing a genome from an index of 3 682 E. coli genomes took 54 seconds instead of 13 minutes for a rebuild, and adding one took about a minute. On AllTheBacteria, with 192 billion k -mers and 12 733 species, extracting M. tuberculosis , with 180 094 genomes, took less than four hours, and set operations then traced contamination of its color, some of which the next release of AllTheBacteria still contains. Our work turns large colored k -mer indexes from static snapshots of a collection into resources that can be maintained as the collection evolves. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LoreDepuydt/colored-sbwt-setops .

research.abstract: Abstract Background Apolipoprotein B (apoB) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) are established biomarkers of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) that tend to be closely correlated. However, some individuals have discordant apoB and LDL-C. We evaluated whether apoB/LDL-C discordance is associated with elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), a key marker of systemic inflammation, in a nationally representative sample. Methods and Results We analyzed cross-sectional data of 2226 adults aged 20 years or older from the 2015 to 2016 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete apoB, LDL-C, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP). LDL-C and apoB were converted to survey-weighted z scores, and discordance was the residual of apoB regressed on LDL-C. Participants were classified as apoB-high, LDL-C-high, or concordant (reference). The association of discordance group with elevated hs-CRP ( > 3 mg/L) was estimated with survey-weighted logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and diabetes. Discordance was present in 26.4% of adults (13.7% apoB-higher, 12.6% LDL-C-higher). Elevated hs-CRP prevalence differed by discordance group: 47.6% (95% CI, 37.6–57.7) in the apoB-high group versus 20.5% (12.9–28.1) in the LDL-C-high group and 33.6% (29.7–37.4) in the concordant group. Relative to concordant participants, adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP were higher for apoB-high discordance (odds ratio [OR], 1.58; 95% CI, 1.03–2.45) and lower for LDL-C-high discordance (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.30–0.78). Similar results were obtained among participants not on statin therapy, with apoB-high discordance demonstrating stronger adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP (OR, 2.02; 95% CI, 1.01–4.04). Conclusion Discordantly high apoB relative to LDL-C is associated with systemic inflammation in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults.

research.abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 (CYP) genes form a large and functionally diverse superfamily of heme-thiolate monooxygenases that catalyse the oxidation of endogenous and exogenous compounds. Within this superfamily, CYP4 enzymes primarily act on fatty acids, substrates central to energy metabolism. Sustained flight and long distance migration in birds rely on efficient fatty acid use, making CYP4 a pertinent system for examining how lipid associated functions may vary across avian lineages. Here, we characterised the evolution of CYP4 genes across 363 avian whole genomes, representing over 90% of bird families, to investigate patterns of molecular evolution and their association with ecological and life history variation. We identified four CYP4 subfamilies and analysed sequence evolution using site-models, branch-models, and branch-site models. Our analyses revealed conserved elements of the avian CYP4 repertoire alongside lineage-specific heterogeneity in selective constraint. Several amino acid sites under positive selection were located within substrate recognition sites, regions influencing substrate binding and catalysis. Branch-model analyses identified trait-associated variation in selective pressure across feeding habits, migration and primary lifestyle, with gene-specific patterns. Migration-associated differences in ω remained below one, indicating variation in the strength of selective constraint among migration categories. Branch-site analyses revealed evidence of episodic positive selection associated with migratory lineages. Overall, these results highlight site-specific adaptive evolution within CYP4 genes alongside broader variation in selective constraint, providing insight into the evolution of lipid associated metabolic pathways during avian diversification.

research.abstract: Comparative genomic data can be used to look for substitutions in coding sequences that are associated with the variation of a particular phenotypic trait. A few statistical methods have been proposed to do so for phenotypes represented by discrete values. For continuous traits, no such statistical approach has been proposed, and researchers have resorted to sensible but uncharacterized criteria. Here, we investigate a phylogenetic model for coding sequences where amino acid preferences at a site are given by a continuous function of a quantitative trait. This function is inferred from the amino acids and the trait values in extant species and requires inferred point estimates of ancestral values of the trait at internal nodes. For detecting sites whose evolution is associated with this trait, we use a significance test against the hypothesis that amino acid preference does not depend on the trait. This procedure is compared to simpler strategies on simulated alignments. It displays an increased recall for low false positive rates, which is of special importance for performing whole-genome scans. This comes however at a much higher computational cost, and we suggest using a simple test to filter promising candidate sites. We then revisit a dataset of alignments for 62 species of mammals, using longevity as a phenotypic trait. We apply our method to three protein families that have previously been proposed to display sites associated with variation in lifespan in mammals. Using a graphical representation extracted from the detailed phylogenetic analysis of candidate sites, we suggest that the evidence for this in the sequence data alone is weak. The proposed method has been added to our Pelican software. It is available at https://gitlab.in2p3.fr/phoogle/pelican and can now be used with both discrete and continuous phenotypes to search for sites associated with phenotypic variation, on data sets with thousands of alignments.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Hepatic tuberculosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation that may mimic hepatobiliary malignancy or complex cystic lesions, resulting in diagnostic challenges. Case Presentation: A 36-year-old Filipino woman without recognized immunocompromising conditions presented with fever, weight loss, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging showed a multiloculated cystic lesion in hepatic segments V/VI with focal biliary prominence. Liver biopsy demonstrated necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with focally positive Ziehl-Neelsen staining. Tissue MTB-PCR detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis without rifampicin resistance, and culture confirmed M. tuberculosis complex susceptible to streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol. CT chest showed diffuse bilateral micronodules in a miliary pattern; initial sputum smear and PCR were negative, but final sputum culture became positive at 6 weeks. Standard 2HRZE/4HR therapy was initiated, with clinical and biochemical improvement at 1 month. Conclusion: Hepatic tuberculosis should be considered in atypical cystic hepatic lesions, and tissue diagnosis is essential to avoid unnecessary invasive procedures.

research.abstract: BackgroundLinkage of infectious-disease surveillance data to mortality records is important for estimating long-term outcomes, but incomplete personal identifiers present methodological challenges. We developed and validated a deterministic linkage framework for linking the National Tuberculosis Surveillance System (NTBS) with Office for National Statistics (ONS) mortality records. MethodsTB notifications in England from 2001-2024 were linked to ONS mortality records using 12 sequential matching rules based on combinations of NHS number, date of birth, name, postcode, sex and phonetic matching. Linkage outputs underwent person-level deduplication and clerical review. Precision and recall were estimated, and potential linkage bias assessed by variation in identifier completeness and linkage success. Confirmed false-positive links identified during validation were removed from the analytical dataset. ResultsAmong 151,965 TB notifications, 28,060 initial links were identified. Following deduplication, validation and refinement, 26,937 linked notifications were retained. Estimated precision increased from 97.7% to 99.2% (95% CI 96.8-100.0) following removal of false-positive links; estimated recall was 98.1% (95% CI 95.4-98.6%). More than 90% of links used NHS-number-based match keys. PDS enrichment increased NHS-number availability and enabled additional NHS-number-based links, although a small proportion linked to different ONS records following enrichment. NHS number availability and linkage success differed across demographic and social groups, demonstrating differential linkage. ConclusionsA hierarchical deterministic approach combined with targeted validation achieved high linkage accuracy while identifying and addressing differential linkage. This provides a transparent framework for future NTBS-ONS linkage and may be adaptable to other surveillance systems where comparable identifiers are available. Key messagesO_LIHierarchical deterministic linkage achieved high precision (>99%) and recall (>96%) when linking tuberculosis notifications to mortality records. C_LIO_LIValidation demonstrated that high linkage accuracy can be achieved using routinely collected identifiers within national surveillance data. C_LIO_LIThe validated linkage provides a robust framework for mortality ascertainment and long-term outcome monitoring within tuberculosis surveillance. C_LI

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently co-occur, but their shared genetic susceptibility and directional associations remain unclear. Methods We analyzed European-ancestry genome-wide association study (GWAS) data for ADHD (38,691 cases; 186,843 controls) and BPD (12,339 cases; 1,041,717 controls). Linkage disequilibrium score regression, conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR), bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR), MR accounting for linkage disequilibrium and sample overlap (MR-LAP), Causal Analysis Using Summary Effect estimates (CAUSE), colocalization, and Sum of Single Effects (SuSiE) fine-mapping assessed genetic sharing and directionality. Results Genetic correlation was substantial (r_g = 0.733). ConjFDR identified 48 shared loci; 36 (75%) showed concordant directions in both phenotype-specific comparisons. Functional annotation implicated axon guidance, oxidative phosphorylation, and developing midbrain cells. ADHD-to-BPD MR was positive (22 instruments; inverse-variance weighted beta = 0.487, SE = 0.082, p = 3.27 × 10^-9), persisting after outlier removal, MR-LAP correction, and exclusion of two instruments at colocalized loci. Reverse MR was positive (five instruments; beta = 0.303, SE = 0.112, p = 6.83 × 10^-3) but heterogeneous and variant-sensitive. CAUSE favored directional over sharing-only models in both directions (delta ELPD = 6.98 and 5.92, respectively). SuSiE colocalization supported shared signals at rs17576773, rs9969232, and rs4727799. Conclusions ADHD and BPD exhibit extensive genetic overlap involving 48 shared loci and convergent evidence of directional associations. Findings across complementary methods more consistently support an ADHD-to-BPD relationship, suggesting that shared genetic susceptibility alone may not fully explain their co-occurrence.

research.abstract: Acrosin (ACR) and transmembrane protease serine 12 (TMPRSS12) are sperm-related S1/trypsin-like serine proteases involved in mammalian male fertility, but their evolutionary relationship in vertebrates remains unclear. Here, we combined phylogenetic, synteny, selection-pressure, and transcriptomic analyses to investigate their evolutionary origin and divergence. OHNOLOGS v2 identified ACR-TMPRSS12 as a candidate ohnolog pair with strong outgroup support, and OrthoFinder placed their duplication in the ancestor of jawed vertebrates. Phylogenetic analyses recovered ACR and TMPRSS12 as reciprocally monophyletic sister clades, consistent with an ancient duplication that may be associated with the two rounds of whole-genome duplication (2R-WGD). Their subsequent evolutionary trajectories differed markedly. ACR was retained in chondrichthyans, sarcopterygians, tetrapods, and acipenseriforms, whereas its widespread loss in other actinopterygians largely coincided with acrosome loss, although bichirs retained the acrosome but lacked ACR. TMPRSS12 was widely retained across jawed vertebrates but showed relaxed selection in Poeciliidae and independent losses in Sebastes and Takifugu. Both genes exhibited testis-biased transcript expression, and their proteins retained a relatively conserved trypsin-like catalytic domain. These findings reveal contrasting patterns of gene retention between ACR and TMPRSS12 and lineage-specific variation in selective constraints on TMPRSS12, consistent with their divergence following an ancient duplication event.

research.abstract: Background Aging-related genes (ARGs) may contribute to immune heterogeneity in tuberculosis (TB), but their diagnostic and biological relevance remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify TB-associated ARG transcripts, characterize their immune and molecular correlates, and evaluate their exploratory diagnostic performance across prespecified cohorts. Patients and methods Public TB transcriptomic cohorts were analyzed together with a local bulk RNA-seq cohort comprising 5 TB patients and 5 controls and a local single-cell RNA-seq cohort comprising 3 active TB patients and 3 controls. The local cohorts were selected using random sampling. Age-adjusted differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, machine-learning-based feature selection, immune-infiltration analysis, consensus clustering, single-cell annotation, and Comparative Toxicogenomics Database-based compound-gene screening were performed. Results GSE83456 included 45 TB patients and 61 controls. Age-adjusted differential expression identified 189 differentially expressed genes, and the intersection of DEGs, ARGs, and blue-module genes yielded 11 discovery candidates. Nested model selection in GSE83456 identified a naive Bayes classifier based on STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14. Across five repeated stratified nested cross-validation runs, the mean AUC was 0.962, with a repeat-level range of 0.954-0.969. Balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 0.926, 0.911, 0.941, and 0.928, respectively. Exploratory evaluations included GSE19439, GSE34608, GSE62525, GSE19444, and the local RNA-seq cohort. Consensus clustering separated TB samples into two ARG-associated subgroups with distinct immune-infiltration and pathway-activity profiles. CIBERSORT analysis identified significant TB-control differences in 9 of 22 inferred immune-cell types. Single-cell analysis demonstrated heterogeneous expression of STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14 across annotated immune-cell subsets. CTD screening generated exploratory compound-gene associations that provide testable hypotheses for future experimental studies. Conclusion Age-adjusted multi-cohort analysis identified candidate ARG-associated TB markers and immune patterns. STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14 are candidate markers rather than clinically validated biomarkers and require independent experimental and clinical validation.

research.abstract: Background Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal–lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. Methods During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. Results Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. Discussion Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: Abstract Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) H9N2 viruses are endemic in poultry across Bangladesh, causing substantial economic losses and posing a persistent zoonotic risk. Although genetic surveillance has documented ongoing viral evolution, the relationship between genetic diversification and antigenic change remains poorly understood. This study investigated the genetic diversity, reassortment, and antigenic characteristics of contemporary H9N2 viruses circulating in Bangladesh. Phylogenetic analysis of 219 sampled sequences revealed three genetically distinct monophyletic haemagglutinin (HA) G-lineage sub-groups, each characterised by unique amino acid substitutions. In contrast, neuraminidase (NA) displayed similar genetic diversity without distinct phylogenetic clusters. A dual-metric analysis of paired HA and NA phylogenies identified 20 putative reassortant H9N2 viruses. Further analysis showed that genetic diversity was geographically structured; however, all three HA subgroups co-circulated across multiple regions, and some live bird markets contained representatives of all three groups simultaneously, suggesting that live bird markets may facilitate mixing between genetically distinct viruses, and create opportunities for reassortment among otherwise geographically separated strains. Despite substantial genetic diversity and reassortment, all viruses remained antigenically similar based on haemagglutination inhibition and virus neutralisation assays. However, a representative strain from one subgroup induced significantly lower homologous and heterologous antibody titres, suggesting reduced immunogenicity. Our findings demonstrate a notable disconnect between genetic evolution and antigenic change in Bangladeshi H9N2 viruses. While reassortment and genetic diversification continue to shape viral populations, antigenic properties remain largely conserved, supporting the continued relevance of current vaccine strategies while highlighting the importance of ongoing genetic and antigenic surveillance. Importance Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) H9N2 viruses remain endemic in Bangladesh and continue to evolve through genetic diversification and reassortment. This study demonstrates that, despite the emergence of three distinct HA genetic subgroups and frequent reassortment events, contemporary Bangladeshi H9N2 viruses remain antigenically conserved. These findings reveal an important disconnect between genetic evolution and antigenic change, indicating that genetic divergence alone may not predict vaccine effectiveness. The co-circulation of multiple viral subgroups within live bird markets highlights their role as hubs for viral mixing and reassortment, emphasizing the need for targeted surveillance in these settings. While current vaccine strategies are likely to remain effective against circulating strains, the identification of a subgroup with reduced immunogenicity underscores the importance of continued monitoring of both genetic and phenotypic traits. Together, these findings provide critical evidence to support risk assessment, vaccine evaluation, and avian influenza control programmes in Bangladesh and beyond.

research.abstract: Abstract Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive. Clinical trial registration Not applicable.

research.abstract: Abstract Bacteria can evolve resistance to bacteriophage attack via mutations that alter phage receptors on the cell surface. Flagellotropic phages bind to motility-enabling flagella, creating a potential evolutionary trade-off, since losing flagellar function can reduce fitness in many environments. Phage-resistance studies typically characterize this trade-off using population-mean phenotypes, but selection can act on, and reshape, the underlying single-cell distribution of a trait in ways that mean values alone do not capture. Here, we exploit the well-developed and experimentally tractable model system of Escherichia coli –phage χ (chi) to ask how evolved resistance to a flagellotropic phage reshapes single-cell motility phenotypes, not just their population averages. We experimentally evolved E. coli populations under selection by χ, on soft-agar swim plates which favor motility. Whole genome sequencing revealed early emergence of non-motile mutants with disrupted motility genes, followed by motile, χ-resistant mutants carrying flagellin mutations. Swim-plate assays and single-cell tracking revealed heterogeneous motility outcomes among resistant lineages: some recovered or exceeded ancestor-level motility while others swam slower than ancestors, demonstrating that trade-offs and trade-ups can both arise from selection by the same phage—an outcome rarely captured in a single phage-resistance study. Single-cell tracking further showed that resistant lineages evolved increased tumble bias and altered swimming speed distributions, revealing shifts in trait heterogeneity invisible to mean-based measures. At the ensemble level, resistant mutants also showed remodeled kinase-response output in the upstream chemotaxis signaling pathway, indicating that resistance reshapes motility behavior both through receptor-level and signaling-level adaptation. Together, these findings demonstrate that evolved phage-resistance reshapes the receptor-linked (motility) phenotype across multiple phenotypic scales: from single-cell behavioral distributions to signaling network output, producing diverse and previously undocumented evolutionary outcomes under combined selection pressures. Author Summary Bacteria often rely on flagella, tail-like appendages that enable swimming, to move toward nutrients and escape undesirable environments. Many viruses that infect and kill bacteria (lytic bacteriophages) exploit these motility-enabling flagella to attach to bacterial cells, creating an evolutionary dilemma: a bacterium can become resistant by losing its flagella, but this sacrifices its ability to move. We used experimental evolution to study how motile bacteria respond to attack by such phages. By exposing E. coli to the flagellum-targeting phage χ over many generations, we found that resistance evolved in two stages. Bacteria first became resistant by losing motility entirely, but soon after, motile χ-resistant variants emerged carrying mutations in flagellin, the flagellum’s main building block. Some of these motile-resistant lineages swam even better than their ancestor, while others swam worse, revealing diverse evolutionary solutions to the same selective pressure. Using fluorescence-based signaling measurements, we found that resistant bacteria also altered the internal chemical signaling that controls swimming behavior, not just the physical structure targeted by the phage. These findings reveal how pathogens can retain or even enhance mobility while evading phage attack, with implications for designing phage-based therapies to treat infections by motile pathogens.

research.abstract: Abstract Introgression introduced deeply diverged archaic variation into modern human populations and contributed to local adaptation. In Indigenous American populations, however, the landscape of adaptive introgression remains poorly resolved. Genome-wide scans have reported numerous candidate loci, but complex demographic histories and recent admixture make genuine signals difficult to distinguish from false positives. Here, we systematically re-evaluated previously reported candidates of adaptive introgression in Peruvians using a multilayered framework and refined more than 150 putative signals to 25 high-confidence candidate loci with concordant evidence of Neanderthal- or Denisovan-like ancestry and positive selection. Using ancestral recombination graph (ARG) approaches, we inferred selection onset windows for 21 loci. These onsets were non-uniformly distributed across Peruvian population history, revealing temporally dynamic selection without robust evidence for a fixed number of discrete waves. Together with pre-Columbian ancient DNA evidence, the inferred histories support the inheritance of the candidate adaptive archaic haplotypes through ancestral Native American populations rather than first introduction through post-Columbian admixture. Functional analyses identified network-level signals consistent with polygenic selection in lipid metabolic and immune-related pathways, elevated regulatory effects predicted across archaic haplotypes, and occasional coding variation of potential functional relevance, including a missense variant at the immune-related gene CXCR4 . Our results show that archaic introgressed variation remained evolutionarily important and available to selection long after introgression, providing a reservoir of genetic variation that could be repeatedly recruited by selection at different points in American population history. Significance Statement Archaic variants reached the Americas through populations already carrying Neanderthal and Denisovan ancestry, offering an opportunity to study adaptation far from the original contact zone. Scans of American populations have reported more putative adaptive introgression loci than realistically expected, partly because the complex demographic histories make true signals difficult to distinguish from false positives. Reconstructing selection histories at credible loci may in turn help constrain that history. Here we identify 25 high-confidence candidate regions in Peruvians, among which 21 have inferred selection onsets predating European contact, and archaic-associated alleles from all 25 are present in pre-Columbian American ancient genomes. Functional analyses find pathway-level selection signals, predicted regulatory effects, and occasional evolutionarily interesting missense variants, including at the immune-related gene CXCR4 .

research.abstract: Introduction TB incidence in Suriname has remained stable over the last decade. Understanding transmission patterns is essential for developing effective TB control strategies to interrupt ongoing transmission. Methods We conducted a descriptive analysis of routinely collected demographic and clinical data combined with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data. Patients were classified into large (>6 patients) clusters, small (2-6 patients) clusters, or as non-clustered cases (unique). Bivariate and multivariable analyses compared patients in large clusters with those in small clusters and non-clustered patients. Epidemiological links obtained through patient interviews were compared with WGS findings. Results Of 698 TB patients notified during 2019-2024, WGS data were available for 368 (53%); 85% belonged to a genomic cluster. Indigenous ethnicity was inversely associated with membership in a large versus a small cluster (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 0.3; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.1-0.6). Compared with non-clustered cases, patients in large clusters were more likely to report illicit drug use (aOR = 3.0; 95% CI = 1.1-8.9). Conclusion WGS provided detailed insights into Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission in Suriname. Illicit drug use was associated with membership in large transmission clusters, highlighting the need for early case finding and strengthened collaboration between TB and substance-use services.

items.summary: Background: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker for pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors, but limitations in sensitivity and universally accepted detection criteria remain. We evaluated multimodal ctDNA detection using a novel composite scoring framework integrating mutation, copy number, and fragmentomic analysis in longitudinal plasma and CSF samples from children…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker for pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors, but limitations in sensitivity and universally accepted detection criteria remain. We evaluated multimodal ctDNA detection using a novel composite scoring framework integrating mutation, copy number, and fragmentomic analysis in longitudinal plasma and CSF samples from children with CNS tumors. Methods Tumor, blood and/or CSF samples were collected from pediatric CNS tumor patients. DNA was extracted from plasma, CSF, tumor, and whole blood. All samples underwent targeted and whole genome sequencing. Plasma and CSF samples were evaluated for ctDNA positivity—defined by a composite score ≥2—utilizing a tri-modal approach of whole genome sequencing for copy number alterations and fragmentomics and targeted sequencing. Results The cohort included 28 patients: medulloblastoma (39%), diffuse midline glioma (25%), high-grade glioma (18%), pilocytic astrocytoma (11%), and ependymoma (7%). A total of 140 plasma and 27 CSF samples were collected longitudinally. Combining all three modalities identified ctDNA in 70% of CSF and 17% of plasma samples, exceeding rates achieved by any single modality alone. Post-diagnosis plasma ctDNA positivity was significantly associated with worse progression-free and overall survival. CSF demonstrated significantly higher ctDNA signal intensity than plasma across all assay modalities. Conclusions A multimodal composite scoring approach improves longitudinal ctDNA detection in pediatric CNS tumors. Although CSF remains the most sensitive biofluid, plasma ctDNA reflects disease progression in select patients. These findings support integrated, multimodal liquid biopsy strategies for disease monitoring and highlight the need for prospective validation of standardized detection criteria. KEY POINTS Multimodal profiling of longitudinal plasma and CSF samples improves circulating tumor DNA detection in pediatric CNS tumors. Post-diagnosis plasma ctDNA positivity was associated with inferior progression-free survival despite the known challenges of plasma-based detection in pediatric CNS tumors. IMPORTANCE OF THE STUDY Pediatric brain tumors are among the most devastating childhood cancers, yet tools for non-invasive disease monitoring remain limited. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) detected in blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) offers a window into tumor biology without repeated surgery or biopsy. Here, we developed a multimodal scoring framework combining mutation analysis, copy number profiling, and DNA fragmentomics to standardize ctDNA detection across biofluids. Integrating all three methods improved detection beyond any single approach alone, and plasma ctDNA positivity was associated with significantly worse survival outcomes. These findings support the continued development of multimodal liquid biopsy as a clinical tool for disease monitoring in pediatric brain tumors.

items.summary: Dietary ethanol has long been proposed as a selective force shaping the diets and physiology of tropical frugivores and nectarivores, yet this idea has rested on measurements from only a few species and sites. Here, we present the first global survey of ethanol in wild fruits and flowers (591 and 37 species, respectively, across 18 countries) and test ecological and phylogenetic predictors of its…

research.abstract: Dietary ethanol has long been proposed as a selective force shaping the diets and physiology of tropical frugivores and nectarivores, yet this idea has rested on measurements from only a few species and sites. Here, we present the first global survey of ethanol in wild fruits and flowers (591 and 37 species, respectively, across 18 countries) and test ecological and phylogenetic predictors of its variation. We detected ethanol in the ripened fruits of 72% of angiosperm species (211 species, N [≥] 3 per species; 0.021% - 3.9% alcohol by volume (ABV)). Ethanol was also detected in the flowers of 12 species (0.037% - 0.73% ABV). Maximum fruit ethanol varied with temperature, humidity, and phylogenetic relatedness, and it was higher in ripe fruits collected from the forest floor relative to their canopy counterparts. We then extrapolated potential daily ethanol consumption for 10 primate species. Estimated maximum daily ethanol ingestion for primates ranged from negligible to 0.72 g/kg/day on average (equivalent to 5.1 international standard drinks, 10 g ethanol each, for a 70 kg human). Our findings show that ethanol is widespread in plant reproductive tissues and shaped by both phylogeny and environment, supporting the hypothesis that dietary ethanol has been a pervasive selective pressure on fruit- and nectar-feeding animals.

research.abstract: Abstract Ancestral sequences and substitution histories are usually averaged out in phylogenetic inference and are therefore not reported to the user. However, they can be recovered through ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) and stochastic character mapping. By implementing and validating a new ASR and stochastic mapping package compatible with both single-locus and multispecies coalescent analysis, we show how reconstructing substitution histories can enhance the information gained about the tempo and mode of molecular evolution. We observe that known substitution histories (simulated and empirical) are recovered more accurately and precisely on time trees compared with unconstrained and non-ultrametric substitution trees that lack temporal directionality (maximum likelihood and Bayesian). We show that codon-partition models with site-rate heterogeneity, based on the four nucleotide characters, can effectively approximate the histories of synonymous and non-synonymous change, while requiring far less runtime than computationally demanding codon models that require 61 characters. In turn, this provides low-bias estimation of dN/dS that is robust to non-stationarity in GC content, codon usage bias, and nucleotide exchangeability rates. Lastly, using three case studies, we demonstrate how the approach can recover expected patterns in molecular evolution and pathogen transmission: that i) smaller-bodied mammalian species tend to have faster synonymous substitution rates than larger relatives, ii) amino acid substitutions are correlated with 3Di structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and iii) influenza A virus spread more frequently to nearby locations than distant ones, in a major H3N2 outbreak in New Zealand. These three trends were more pronounced when based on count estimates derived from stochastic mapping, relative to parametric rates and distances. Our open-source code comes with a user-friendly graphical interface, as the BeastMap package for BEAST 2; supporting a wide range of clock, site, and tree models and data types – including insertions and deletions – within a Bayesian phylogenetic framework.

research.abstract: Abstract Persistent viral infections provide an extended window for viral evolution, yet their intra-host trajectories across the host lifespan remain underexplored. Here, we tracked the longitudinal evolution of three single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) viruses (Drosophila A virus [DAV], Drosophila C virus [DCV], and Nora virus) and one double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus (Bloomfield virus) during persistent infection in Drosophila melanogaster . By analyzing viral populations across early, intermediate, and late infection stages, we mapped dynamic shifts in the viral quasispecies and the emergence of adaptive mutations. These data demonstrate that long-term persistence drives viral evolution in a viral species-specific manner. DAV evolution was defined by clonal interference, driven by the continuous turnover of competing haplotypes. Nora virus exhibited prolonged evolutionary stasis punctuated by a late-stage sweep, suggesting adaptation to the senescing host environment. In contrast, standard DCV populations were locked under strong purifying selection, where no adaptive mutations were detected. However, this constraint collapsed in high-titer DCV infections, triggering extensive mutational diversification. Distinct from the ssRNA dynamics, the multi-segmented dsRNA Bloomfield virus maintained higher sequence fidelity and a stable genomic formula. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that viral evolution during persistent infection is governed by the interplay between specific host-pathogen interactions and the physiological decline of the host.

research.abstract: Empyema necessitans is a rare complication of pleural infection in which infected pleural fluid extends through the parietal pleura into the surrounding soft tissues. We report the case of a 32-year-old man of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom who presented with worsening right-sided pleuritic chest pain, several months of night sweats, and a persistent dry cough. Five months earlier, he had been treated for right-sided pneumonia complicated by a pleural effusion, with persistent radiographic abnormalities on follow-up. Examination revealed reduced right-sided air entry and a tender, fluctuant swelling over the right posterior chest wall. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a posterior pleural collection extending through the chest wall into the adjacent paraspinal musculature, consistent with empyema necessitans. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded frank purulent fluid. Routine bacterial, anaerobic, and fungal cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli were not seen on initial microscopy; however, mycobacterial culture became positive after seven days, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Whole-genome sequencing subsequently identified a lineage 1 East-African-Indian-Ocean isolate with predicted susceptibility to first-line antituberculous agents. Four-drug antituberculous therapy was commenced, with subsequent clinical and radiological improvement. This case highlights chest wall swelling as an unusual presentation of tuberculosis and emphasizes the importance of cross-sectional imaging and targeted mycobacterial testing in establishing the diagnosis.

research.abstract: Polygonatum zanlanscianense Pamp. is a perennial herb (Asparagaceae) endemic to China, whose rhizomes are used in folk medicine as a substitute for Polygonati Rhizoma. Although its plastome has been reported, the mitogenome remained uncharacterized. Here, we assembled and annotated the complete linear mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense and analysed its gene repertoire, codon usage, repeats, RNA editing sites, MTPTs, synteny, phylogeny and Ka/Ks. The 689,491-bp mitogenome (GC 46.23%) encodes 56 genes: 36 PCGs, three rRNA genes and 17 tRNA genes. Codon usage is biased toward A/U-ending codons. We identified 68 SSRs, 25 tandem repeats, 1366 dispersed repeat pairs, 585 predicted C-to-U editing sites concentrated at the first and second codon positions, and 30 MTPT fragments accounting for 2.24% of the mitogenome. Phylogenetic analysis placed P. zanlanscianense as sister to Polygonatum kingianum Collett & Hemsl. Median Ka/Ks was below 1 for 33 of the 35 genes analysed; although rpl5 and ccmB showed elevated ratios, branch-site tests did not support positive selection. This first mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense provides genomic resources for comparative genomic, phylogenetic and medicinal studies in Polygonatum.

research.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis Diagnosis delays among tuberculosis patients can worsen infection transmission, disease severity, and mortality risk. Identifying factors influencing delays is crucial due to its persistence across healthcare levels and communities. The study identify determinants of tuberculosis diagnosis delay among patients attending public health facility of Metekel zone, Northwest Ethiopia:2023 Methods: An unmatched case-control study was conducted in Metekel zone health facilities from March to April 2023, involving 210 tuberculosis patients (103 cases, 107 controls) selected through systematic sampling. Data collected through structured questionnaires and STATA used for analysis, including bi-variable and multi-variable logistic regressions. Variables with p-value < 0.25 in bi-variable analysis were included in the final model after checking model fitness and multicollinearity. Results: Overall, 210 tuberculosis patients were included in the study. The following independent variables were associated diagnosis delay of tuberculosis: TB patients who travel greater than 10km (AOR: 2.941, (95 % CI: 1.509, 5.731); TB patients who are living at rural area (AOR: 4.135, 95 % CI :1.759, 9.723); TB patients who prior visit in holly-water and traditional medicine [AOR: 2.978, (95% CI: 1.292, 6.863); poor knowledge about TB [AOR: 2.826, (95% CI: 1.404, 5.687)]. Conclusion: Tuberculosis diagnosis delay is a major challenge to eliminate tuberculosis by breaking the chain of transmission. This study can be attributed to factors including place of residence being rural, poor knowledge about tuberculosis, non-health facility initial actions upon symptom onset, and far distance to health institutions. Recognizing these determinants helps in identifying and addressing barriers inhibiting early diagnosis, potentially improving healthcare access and promoting more timely diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis patients.
